name: 1 Corinthians
subtitle: A Wisdom Made of Scripture
howToRead: Writing to a fractious church enamored of cleverness, Paul argues that the wisdom of God is the crucified Christ — and he argues it out of Scripture. The opening chapters drive home the point with a chain of citations: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,” “let him who boasts boast in the Lord,” “no eye has seen what God has prepared,” “he catches the wise in their craftiness.” Then the letter turns the Exodus into a warning written for the church — the fathers under the cloud, baptized into Moses, drinking from the rock that was Christ, falling in the wilderness — and ends on resurrection read straight from the prophets: death swallowed up in victory, its sting drawn, the last Adam undoing the first. The chips beside each passage name the Scripture underneath it — solid for a formal quotation, dashed for an allusion, dotted for a fainter echo, ◇ for a figural pattern that borrows no words. A lighter chip and a trailing ? mark an echo that is faint or contested. Where Paul follows the Greek of the Septuagint against the Hebrew, both readings are shown.

pericopes.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes, to the assembly of God which is at Corinth; those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

echoes.text: and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel.”
echoes.note: The address to those 'sanctified... called to be saints' transfers Israel's vocation as a 'holy nation' set apart for God to the Corinthian assembly. The lexical pairing of calling and holiness coheres thematically with the Sinai constitution of a consecrated people; the volume is modest because Paul cites no formula, but the figural availability of Exodus 19 to a Jewish reader is high.

echoes.text: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth. For I am Yahweh who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
echoes.note: 'Sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints' echoes the Holiness Code refrain 'be holy, for I am holy,' in which Israel's status as God's set-apart people is grounded in God's own holiness. Recurrence is strong across Leviticus 19-20, and the thematic coherence of consecration as gift-and-summons fits Paul's idiom of being made holy in Christ.

echoes.text: It will happen, that he who is left in Zion, and he who remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, even everyone who is written among the living in Jerusalem;
echoes.note: The phrase 'called holy' (kalein hagion) for the eschatological remnant in Zion resonates with 'called to be saints.' The verbal link is suggestive in the LXX, but the volume is faint and the motif is widely diffused, so it is offered only as a contested resonance.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: 'All who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place' reworks Joel's 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved,' transferring the divine Name to Jesus. Volume is high (distinctive idiom 'call on the name'), recurrence strong in Paul (Rom 10:13), and the eschatological-salvation theme coheres tightly with the surrounding 'day of the Lord' language.

echoes.text: A son was also born to Seth, and he named him Enosh. At that time men began to call on Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: The idiom 'call on the name of the LORD' first appears at the dawn of worship in Genesis 4:26 and runs through the patriarchal narratives (Gen 12:8; 13:4). It supplies the deep semantic background for Paul's phrase, though Joel is the proximate and more specific source.

echoes.text: I will take the cup of salvation, and call on Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: The cultic act of 'calling on the name of the LORD' in the thanksgiving psalter underlies the worship-language of 'all who call on the name.' Recurrence within the Psalms is notable, but the volume here is faint relative to the Joel allusion that controls the phrase.

echoes.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
echoes.note: Zephaniah's promise that the nations will 'call on the name of the LORD' with one accord matches Paul's universalizing 'in every place, both theirs and ours.' The thematic coherence of an ingathered people invoking the Name is good, but the verbal contact is light and the motif overlaps with Joel.

pericopes.text: I always thank my God concerning you, for the grace of God which was given you in Christ Jesus; that in everything you were enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge; even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you: so that you come behind in no gift; waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ; who will also confirm you until the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ, our Lord.

echoes.text: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light.
echoes.note: The repeated 'day of our Lord Jesus Christ' (v.8) draws on the prophetic 'day of the LORD' tradition, of which Amos is the classic warning text. Thematic coherence is strong: Paul reframes the eschatological day as the point of vindication 'blameless,' and the recurrence of yom YHWH across the prophets gives the motif high availability.

echoes.text: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'The day of our Lord' as the eschatological revelation aligns with Joel's 'great and terrible day of the LORD,' the same chapter Paul has just drawn on in v.2. The internal recurrence (Joel within the immediate context) strengthens the case for a Joel-shaped horizon, though the phrase is generic enough to be merely traditional.

echoes.text: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly.
echoes.note: Zephaniah's 'great day of the LORD is near' is among the most concentrated 'day of the LORD' oracles and feeds the same prophetic reservoir behind v.8. The volume is low because Paul names no specific feature of Zephaniah's day, but the motif's availability is high.

echoes.text: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;
echoes.note: 'Who can stand when he appears?'—the day that tests and refines—coheres with Paul's hope that the Corinthians be 'confirmed... blameless in the day.' The forensic-purgative coloring of being found unblamable resonates, but the connection is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: 'God is faithful, through whom you were called' (v.9) echoes the covenant formula that 'the LORD your God is the faithful God who keeps covenant.' Volume is good on the distinctive predicate 'faithful' applied to God as the guarantor of a calling, and the covenant-keeping theme coheres with Paul's assurance of preservation to the end.

echoes.text: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.
echoes.note: The Song of Moses names God 'faithful (pistos) and without iniquity,' a likely LXX source for Paul's 'God is faithful.' Recurrence of the divine epithet pistos in Deuteronomy supports availability, though the phrase had become a settled liturgical commonplace.

pericopes.text: Now I beg you, brothers, through the name of our Lord, Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgment. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who are from Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you. Now I mean this, that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” and, “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul? I thank God that I baptized none of you, except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one should say that I had baptized you into my own name. (I also baptized the household of Stephanas; besides them, I don’t know whether I baptized any other.) For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the Good News—not in wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ wouldn’t be made void.

echoes.text: Take wise men of understanding and well known according to your tribes, and I will make them heads over you.”
echoes.note: Paul's plea that they be 'perfected together in the same mind and the same judgment,' against 'contentions,' faintly recalls Moses' appointment of wise leaders to adjudicate strife among a quarreling people. The thematic coherence (concord versus faction) is reasonable, but verbal contact is slight and the appeal to unity is a general topos.

echoes.text: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!
echoes.note: 'How good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity' supplies a scriptural ideal of fraternal concord behind Paul's exhortation that 'brothers' avoid divisions. The resonance is thematic and the term 'brothers' is shared, but the volume is faint and the motif diffuse.

pericopes.text: For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, I will bring the discernment of the discerning to nothing.” Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the lawyer of this world? Hasn’t God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For seeing that in the wisdom of God, the world through its wisdom didn’t know God, it was God’s good pleasure through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe. For Jews ask for signs, Greeks seek after wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified; a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”
echoes.note: Verse 19 quotes with formula ('it is written') Isaiah 29:14 LXX: 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart/bring to nothing.' Volume is maximal (verbatim citation), and the thematic coherence is exact: God's overturning of human sagacity is the engine of Paul's whole cross-versus-wisdom argument.

echoes.text: The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish. The counsel of the wisest counselors of Pharaoh has become stupid. How do you say to Pharaoh, “I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings?” Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you now; and let them know what Yahweh of Armies has purposed concerning Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Where is the wise?' (v.20) recalls the taunt against Egypt's counselors: 'Where then are your wise men?... let them tell.' The interrogative form mocking discredited sages is distinctive, and recurrence within Isaiah's wisdom-polemic strengthens coherence with Paul's rhetorical questions about the wise of this age.

echoes.text: Your heart will meditate on the terror. Where is he who counted? Where is he who weighed? Where is he who counted the towers?
echoes.note: 'Where is the scribe? Where is the one who weighed?' supplies the closest LXX template for Paul's triad 'Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater?' The naming of the 'scribe (grammateus)' is the load-bearing verbal link, and the context of a vanished officialdom after divine deliverance coheres with Paul's point.

echoes.text: He leads counselors away stripped. He makes judges fools.
echoes.note: Job's hymn declares that God 'leads counselors away stripped and makes fools of judges,' overturning the wisdom of the prudent (cf. Job 12:20, 'he takes away the discernment of the elders'). The thematic coherence with God 'making foolish the wisdom of this world' is strong, and the recurrence of the divine reversal-of-sages motif supports a real echo.

echoes.text: who frustrates the signs of the liars, and makes diviners mad; who turns wise men backward, and makes their knowledge foolish;
echoes.note: 'Frustrating the signs of liars and making fools of diviners, turning wise men back and making their knowledge foolish'—this Deutero-Isaiah oracle nearly paraphrases v.20's 'Hasn't God made foolish the wisdom of this world?' The verbal cluster (wise/foolish/knowledge) is dense and the polemic against pretended wisdom coheres tightly.

echoes.text: The wise men are disappointed. They are dismayed and trapped. Behold, they have rejected Yahweh’s word. What kind of wisdom is in them?
echoes.note: 'The wise men shall be put to shame... they have rejected the word of the LORD, and what wisdom is in them?' parallels Paul's claim that the world's wisdom failed to know God. The shaming of the wise and the linkage of wisdom to receiving God's word cohere, though the verbal contact is moderate.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'A stumbling block to Jews' (v.23) draws on Isaiah's image of the LORD as 'a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' to the houses of Israel. Volume is good on the distinctive 'stumbling/offense' lexeme, recurrence is strong in Paul (Rom 9:33), and the irony of God's saving act becoming an obstacle to Israel coheres precisely.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'tested stone' laid in Zion, paired in Pauline usage with Isaiah 8:14, underlies the 'stumbling block' of v.23 and the foundation-stone motif of the proclaimed Christ. The connection is figural and mediated through Paul's wider stone testimonia rather than directly verbal here.

echoes.text: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously; for I am working a work in your days, which you will not believe though it is told you.
echoes.note: 'I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if told' offers a scriptural template for God accomplishing salvation through means the wise reject as incredible. The thematic coherence with the cross as God's unbelievable 'good pleasure' is suggestive, but the verbal link is faint.
echoes.lxxText: Behold, ye despisers, and look, and wonder marvelously, and vanish: for I work a work in your days, which ye will in no wise believe, though a man declare it to you.

pericopes.text: For you see your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong; and God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that are not, that he might bring to nothing the things that are: that no flesh should boast before God. But of him, you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption: that, according as it is written, “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Verse 31 quotes with formula ('as it is written') Jeremiah 9:24 LXX: 'Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.' Volume is maximal, and the surrounding verses (Jer 9:23, 'let not the wise boast in his wisdom, nor the mighty in his might') govern Paul's entire argument that the wise, mighty, and noble have no ground for boasting before God.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches;
echoes.note: The triad of v.26—'not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble'—directly mirrors Jeremiah 9:23's catalogue 'let not the wise boast in his wisdom, the mighty in his might, the rich in his riches.' The recurrence is structural: Paul builds the catalogue (vv.26-29) precisely to set up the Jeremiah citation in v.31, so the allusion and quotation are a single sustained engagement.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Gideon, “The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’
echoes.note: God reduces Gideon's army 'lest Israel boast... saying, My own hand has saved me'—the paradigm of God choosing weakness so that 'no flesh should boast' (v.29). The thematic coherence is precise (election of the weak to negate human self-glory), and the Gideon narrative supplies a recurrent OT pattern of God shaming the strong through the few.

echoes.text: But I will leave in your midst an afflicted and poor people, and they will take refuge in Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: God's promise to leave 'a people humble and lowly' who take refuge in the LORD's name coheres with God choosing 'the lowly things of the world and the things that are despised.' The remnant of the low and despised as the locus of salvation matches Paul's reversal, and 'name of the LORD' links back to the chapter's calling-language.

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.
echoes.note: Hannah's song—'the LORD makes poor and rich, brings low and exalts; he raises the poor from the dust... to make them sit with princes'—is the canonical hymn of divine status-reversal underlying vv.27-28. Thematic coherence is high and the motif recurs (cf. Ps 113:7), giving strong availability for Paul's exaltation of the low and lowering of the high.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”
echoes.note: Having quoted Isaiah 29:14 at v.19, Paul continues its logic here: God destroys the wisdom of the wise by choosing the foolish 'to shame the wise.' The recurrence of the same Isaianic oracle across the unit (criterion of recurrence) confirms that the wisdom-reversal of vv.27-28 is still being read through Isaiah 29.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will raise to David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely; and this is his name by which he shall be called: Yahweh our righteousness.
echoes.note: Christ 'made to us... righteousness' (v.30) figurally realizes Jeremiah's messianic Branch named 'The LORD is our righteousness.' The distinctive predication of righteousness to the Davidic deliverer coheres with Paul's compressed christological list, and the title's availability in messianic exegesis supports a deliberate figural reading.

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]
echoes.note: Christ 'made to us wisdom from God' (v.30) draws on the personified Wisdom present with God at creation. The wisdom-Christology of vv.24, 30 coheres with the Wisdom tradition, and recurrence in Second-Temple Wisdom literature (Sir 24; Wis 7) makes the identification of Christ with God's Wisdom a well-attested move.

echoes.text: For she is a breath of the power of God, And a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; Therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom as 'a breath of the power of God... a pure emanation of his glory' offers the nearest Second-Temple background for Christ as 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' (v.24) 'made to us wisdom from God.' Availability is strong (deuterocanonical Wisdom was current), and the fusion of power and wisdom in a single divine agency coheres precisely.

echoes.text: Wisdom will praise herself, And will glory in the midst of her people. In the congregation of the Most High will she open her mouth, And glory in the presence of his power. I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, And covered the earth as a mist. I lived in high places, And my throne is in the pillar of the cloud. Alone I compassed the circuit of heaven, And walked in the depth of the abyss. In the waves of the sea, and in all the earth, And in every […]
echoes.note: Sirach's hymn of Wisdom seeking a dwelling among God's people supports the wisdom-Christology of vv.24, 30, where Christ becomes the locus of God's wisdom for believers. The thematic link to personified Wisdom is real, but the verbal volume is faint relative to Proverbs 8 and Wisdom 7.

echoes.text: In Yahweh shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.
echoes.note: 'In the LORD all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory'—pairing justification with glorying/boasting in the LORD—anticipates the v.30-31 link between Christ as righteousness and boasting 'in the Lord.' The conjunction of being made righteous and boasting only in God coheres, though Jeremiah 9 remains the explicit source.

pericopes.text: When I came to you, brothers, I didn’t come with excellence of speech or of wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God. For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling. My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.

echoes.text: Terror and dread falls on them. By the greatness of your arm they are as still as a stone— until your people pass over, Yahweh, until the people pass over who you have purchased.
echoes.note: Paul's self-description 'in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling' (v.3) draws on the stock biblical pairing of fear and trembling, programmatically stated in the Song of the Sea where 'fear and dread' and 'trembling' fall on the nations before God's power. Volume is faint and the idiom is diffuse, but it coheres with Paul's argument that the awe belongs to God's power, not human eloquence. Contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: Serve Yahweh with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
echoes.note: 'Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling' supplies the closest devotional sense of Paul's 'fear and much trembling' (v.3) as the proper posture of a servant before God's power. The verbal overlap is real in the Greek (phobos/tromos) but the phrase is formulaic, so the echo is faint and contested against the wider 'fear and trembling' tradition.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Paul's refusal of 'lofty speech or wisdom' so that faith rests 'in the power of God' (vv.1,5) extends Jeremiah's oracle that the wise must not boast in wisdom but only in knowing the LORD. The theme is carried over from 1 Corinthians 1:31, giving recurrence, but the link here is thematic rather than verbal and so faint.

pericopes.text: We speak wisdom, however, among those who are full grown; yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are coming to nothing. But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden, which God foreordained before the worlds for our glory, which none of the rulers of this world has known. For had they known it, they wouldn’t have crucified the Lord of glory. But as it is written, “Things which an eye didn’t see, and an ear didn’t hear, which didn’t enter into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him.”

echoes.text: Daniel answered, Blessed be the name of God forever and ever; for wisdom and might are his. He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known […]
echoes.note: Paul's 'God's wisdom in a mystery (mysterion), hidden, foreordained before the ages' (vv.7) is steeped in Daniel's Aramaic hymn praising God 'to whom belong wisdom and might,' who 'reveals deep and hidden things.' Daniel is the Septuagintal seedbed for mysterion as divinely hidden-then-revealed knowledge, giving strong coherence with Paul's whole argument; the cluster of wisdom + mystery + revelation supplies recurrence.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
echoes.note: 'There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries' is arguably the direct conceptual source for Paul's claim that God's once-hidden wisdom is now revealed (vv.7,10). The technical use of mysterion for an eschatological secret disclosed by God is distinctively Danielic, lending high coherence even without verbatim quotation.

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]
echoes.note: Wisdom 'foreordained before the ages for our glory' (v.7) evokes the personified Wisdom of Proverbs 8, possessed by the LORD 'at the beginning of his work, before the earth was.' The pre-cosmic, pre-temporal location of God's wisdom is the shared point; Paul transposes the Wisdom tradition christologically, so this is figural as much as verbal.

echoes.text: For she is a breath of the power of God, And a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; Therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness. And she, being one, has power to do all things; And remaining in herself, reneweth all things: And from generation to generation passing into holy souls She makes men friends of God and […]
echoes.note: Paul's hidden divine wisdom destined for the glory of those who love God parallels the Wisdom of Solomon's portrait of Sophia as a pure emanation of God's glory that passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God. The Second-Temple sapiential matrix (availability secure) gives strong coherence; 'for our glory' (v.7) echoes Wisdom's glory-language.

echoes.text: And with you is wisdom, which knows your works, And was present when you were making the world, And which understands what is pleasing in your eyes, And what is right according to your commandments. Send her forth out of the holy heavens, And from the throne of your glory bid her come, That being present with me she may toil with me, And that I may learn what is well-pleasing before you. For she knows all things and has understanding thereof, And in my […]
echoes.note: The motif of a wisdom present with God before the world, inaccessible to human counsel, undergirds Paul's 'wisdom of God in a mystery' that none of the rulers knew (vv.7-8). Wisdom 9 also feeds 2:16 below, giving recurrence across the chapter and strengthening the case for Paul's reliance on this prayer of Solomon.

echoes.text: Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is the King of glory? Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in battle. Lift up your heads, you gates; yes, lift them up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.
echoes.note: 'They would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (v.8) most plausibly draws its title from the repeated 'the King of glory... the LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory.' The transfer of a divine glory-title to the crucified Christ is figural and striking; volume rests on the rare phrase 'of glory' applied to the Lord.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s voice is on the waters. The God of glory thunders, even Yahweh on many waters.
echoes.note: 'The God of glory thunders' offers an alternative scriptural source for Paul's 'Lord of glory' (v.8), part of the same Psalter glory-theophany vocabulary as Psalm 24. The link is faint and overlaps with the stronger Psalm 24 candidate.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
echoes.note: Isaiah's vision of the LORD high and lifted up, his glory filling the earth, lies behind the 'Lord of glory' title (v.8) as a theophanic background; rulers who 'did not know' the glory recall Isaiah's commission to a people who see but do not perceive. The connection is thematic and contested against the more verbally exact Psalm 24.

echoes.text: For from of old men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither has the eye seen a God besides you, who works for him who waits for him.
echoes.note: The explicit citation formula 'as it is written' introduces v.9, 'what no eye has seen, nor ear heard...what God has prepared for those who love him,' which most closely matches Isaiah 64:4 (LXX: God acts for those who wait/love him; eye has not seen a God besides you). This is the controlling source-text, though Paul's wording is conflate and not verbatim with any extant version.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: 'Nor did it enter into the heart of man' (v.9) closely matches Isaiah 65:17 LXX, 'the former things shall not be remembered nor come up into the heart,' suggesting Paul conflated Isaiah 64:4 with the new-creation oracle of Isaiah 65. The shared 'heart' idiom and eschatological 'what God has prepared' give this a strong claim to be part of the quotation's source matrix.

echoes.text: She is with all flesh according to his gift; And he gave her freely to those who love him.
echoes.note: Sirach 1:10, 'he supplied wisdom to those who love him,' has been proposed as a partial source for the closing phrase 'for those who love him' (v.9), since this exact clause is absent from Isaiah. The verbal tie is narrow and the dominant source remains Isaianic, so this is a contested supplementary echo.

pericopes.text: But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man, which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God, except God’s Spirit. But we received, not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we might know the things that were freely given to us by God. Which things also we speak, not in words which man’s wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things.

echoes.text: he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
echoes.note: 'The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God' (v.10) coheres with Daniel's 'he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness.' Within the same chapter Paul has already leaned on Daniel 2 for mystery-language (recurrence), so the depths/revelation motif here reinforces that dependence.

echoes.text: The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.
echoes.note: 'The spirit of the man which is in him' knows 'the things of a man' (v.11) draws on Proverbs 20:27, 'the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inward parts.' The shared verb 'search' and the human spirit as inner knower make this a strong conceptual source for Paul's analogy between man's spirit and God's Spirit.

echoes.text: “Can you fathom the mystery of God? Or can you probe the limits of the Almighty?
echoes.note: 'The deep things of God' that only the Spirit can search (v.10) directly answers Zophar's challenge, 'Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?' Paul affirms what Job's friends deemed impossible, now made possible by the Spirit; the verbal tie to 'deep things of God' is close.

echoes.text: For you will not find the depth of the heart of man, and you will not perceive the things that he thinks. How will you search out God, who has made all these things, and know his mind, and comprehend his purpose? No, my kindred, don’t provoke the Lord our God to anger!
echoes.note: Judith's rebuke, 'you cannot plumb the depth of the human heart...how can you search out God who made all things, or comprehend his mind?' parallels Paul's claim that only the Spirit searches God's depths (vv.10-11) and anticipates 2:16. The Second-Temple availability is secure but the verbal overlap is loose, so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: An oracle. Yahweh’s word concerning Israel. Yahweh, who stretches out the heavens, and lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him says:
echoes.note: 'The spirit of the man which is in him' (v.11) may glance at Zechariah's description of the LORD who 'forms the spirit of man within him,' grounding the human inner spirit Paul invokes. The link is thematic and faint, overlapping with the stronger Proverbs 20:27 candidate.

pericopes.text: Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But he who is spiritual discerns all things, and he himself is judged by no one. “For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?” But we have Christ’s mind.

echoes.text: Who has directed the Spirit of Yahweh, or has taught him as his counselor?
echoes.note: Verse 16 'For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?' is a direct quotation of Isaiah 40:13 LXX ('Who has known the mind of the LORD, and who has been his counselor that he should instruct him?'). The wording tracks the Septuagint closely; Paul deploys the unanswerable rhetorical question, then stunningly claims 'we have the mind of Christ.'

echoes.text: For what man will know the counsel of God? Or who will conceive what the Lord willeth? For the thoughts of mortals are timorous, And our plans are prone to fail. For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, And the earthy frame lies heavy on a mind that is full of cares. And hardly do we divine the things that are on earth, And the things that are close at hand we find with labor; But the things that are in the heavens who ever yet traced out? And who […]
echoes.note: Solomon's prayer, 'For who can know the counsel of God?...who has learned your counsel unless you gave wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit?' undergirds both Paul's contrast of the unspiritual person who cannot receive God's things (v.14) and the Isaiah 40:13 citation (v.16). The pairing of the 'who can know God's mind' question with the gift of the Spirit makes Wisdom 9 a likely mediating source; recurrence with 2:6-9 strengthens it.

echoes.text: Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit wisdom to yourself?
echoes.note: Eliphaz's taunt, 'Have you listened in the council of God, and do you limit wisdom to yourself?' anticipates the rhetorical thrust of v.16, 'who has known the mind of the Lord?' The motif of inaccessible divine counsel is shared, but the verbal link is to Isaiah rather than Job, so this is a faint, contested background echo.

echoes.text: For who has stood in the council of Yahweh, that he should perceive and hear his word? who has marked my word, and heard it?
echoes.note: 'Who has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear his word?' supplies the same prophetic topos of access to the divine mind that Paul invokes in v.16. The thematic coherence with the 'mind of the Lord' question is real but the controlling text is Isaiah 40:13, so this remains a faint supplementary echo.

pericopes.text: Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ. I fed you with milk, not with meat; for you weren’t yet ready. Indeed, not even now are you ready, for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men? For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” aren’t you fleshly?

echoes.text: Whom will he teach knowledge? To whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, and drawn from the breasts?
echoes.note: Paul's contrast of milk for 'babies in Christ' versus solid food evokes Isaiah's taunt about teaching knowledge to those weaned from milk and just drawn from the breasts. Both passages use infancy and weaning as a figure for spiritual immaturity and incapacity to receive deeper instruction. Coherence with Paul's pedagogical-maturity theme is strong, and Isaiah 28 is recurrent in this letter's milieu of prophetic critique, though the verbal link rests on the shared milk/infancy metaphor rather than direct citation.

echoes.text: My doctrine will drop as the rain. My speech will condense as the dew, as the misty rain on the tender grass, as the showers on the herb.
echoes.note: The Song of Moses likens teaching/doctrine to rain and dew dropping as nourishment, a nutritive metaphor for instruction that may underlie Paul's feeding imagery (milk/meat). The connection is thematic rather than verbal and is faint; Isaiah 28:9 is the stronger weaning parallel. Marked low and contested for the nourishment-as-teaching figure only.

echoes.text: “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!
echoes.note: Wisdom's invitation to eat her bread and drink her wine frames spiritual instruction as food and drink, resonating faintly with Paul's milk/solid-food pedagogy. Given chapter 3's larger wisdom-versus-folly argument, the sapiential feeding motif coheres, but the link is diffuse and contested.

pericopes.text: Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed; and each as the Lord gave to him? I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. Now he who plants and he who waters are the same, but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: Paul calls the Corinthians 'God's farming/field,' and the Song of the Vineyard is the paradigmatic OT figure of God's people as a cultivated planting that God tends and from which he expects fruit. The agricultural-people metaphor, with God as the one who ultimately gives growth, coheres with Paul's planting/watering argument. Availability and coherence are strong; the allusion is conceptual, since Paul does not cite the vineyard text directly.

echoes.text: to appoint to those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of Yahweh, that he may be glorified.
echoes.note: Isaiah names the redeemed 'oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he may be glorified.' Paul's image of the church as God's planting that God himself grows for his glory closely matches this 'planting of the LORD' motif. The shared theology that God, not the human planter, is the agent of growth strengthens coherence; the link is allusive rather than quoted.

echoes.text: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
echoes.note: Jeremiah's commission pairs the verbs to build and to plant (and to pluck up and break down) as the dual metaphor for God's work through the prophet. Paul fuses exactly these two figures in 3:9 ('God's farming, God's building'), suggesting dependence on the prophetic building-and-planting idiom. The recurrence of this paired metaphor in Jeremiah (1:10; 24:6; 31:28) makes the echo coherent.

echoes.text: For I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up.
echoes.note: God promises to 'build them and not pull down, plant them and not pluck up,' the same build/plant pairing applied to the restored people. It reinforces the Jeremianic source-pool behind Paul's 'building/farming' fusion in 3:9 but is a secondary witness to the idiom rather than a distinct allusion. Marked low and contested.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The psalm depicts Israel as a vine God planted, transplanted, and tends, another instance of the God-as-cultivator/people-as-planting figure standing behind Paul's 'God's farming.' It is a faint, recurrent background witness rather than a specific source, so it is marked low and contested.

pericopes.text: According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it. But let each man be careful how he builds on it. For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or stubble; each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is. If any man’s work remains which he built on it, he will receive a reward. If any man’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, but as through fire.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: Paul as 'wise master builder' lays a foundation that no one can replace, echoing Isaiah's word that God lays in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone as foundation. The foundation-laying imagery and the singular God-given foundation cohere strongly; Isaiah 28:16 is a stock messianic foundation text in early Christian usage. The allusion is conceptual here, more explicitly cited elsewhere in the NT.

echoes.text: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and refine them as gold and silver; and they shall offer to Yahweh offerings in righteousness.
echoes.note: The Day's fire that 'tests what sort of work each man's work is' draws on Malachi's refiner's fire that purifies and assays metal, separating the genuine from the dross. Paul's gold/silver tested by fire on the Day matches the refiner-and-assayer imagery and the eschatological day of judgment. Coherence with the testing/refining motif is strong.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: Malachi's coming Day burns like an oven and consumes the wicked as stubble, leaving neither root nor branch. Paul's contrast of fire-resistant materials versus 'wood, hay, stubble' burned up on the Day strongly evokes this stubble-consuming day of fire. The shared 'stubble burned on the Day' image makes this a coherent allusion.

echoes.text: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”
echoes.note: God brings a third through the fire, refining them as silver and testing them as gold is tested. Paul's 'tested by fire,' with the survivor saved 'but as through fire' (3:15), coheres with Zechariah's image of passing through refining fire and being purified rather than destroyed. The refine-as-silver/test-as-gold language reinforces the metallurgical testing motif.

echoes.text: The refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, but Yahweh tests the hearts.
echoes.note: The crucible for silver and furnace for gold, with the LORD testing hearts, supplies the proverb that God assays human worth by fire. Paul's 'fire itself will test what sort of work each man's work is' applies this assaying principle to deeds at the Day. The shared furnace/testing logic gives medium coherence.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
echoes.note: Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days with a stream of fire issuing before the throne at judgment may color Paul's 'the Day... revealed in fire.' The link is to the eschatological fire-of-judgment topos rather than a specific verbal borrowing, so it is faint and contested.

echoes.text: Now I have prepared with all my might for the house of my God the gold for the things of gold, and the silver for the things of silver, and the brass for the things of brass, the iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood; onyx stones, and stones to be set, stones for inlaid work, and of various colors, and all kinds of precious stones, and marble stones in abundance.
echoes.note: David's gathering of gold, silver, and precious/costly stones for the temple supplies the very building-materials triad Paul ranks as fire-resistant (gold, silver, costly stones). If Paul's 'building' is the temple (3:16-17), the materials catalogue echoes temple-construction lists. Faint and contested, since such triads are commonplace.

pericopes.text: Don’t you know that you are a temple of God, and that God’s Spirit lives in you? If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, which you are.

echoes.text: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.
echoes.note: God commands a sanctuary 'that I may dwell among them,' the foundational text for the divine indwelling presence. Paul transfers this dwelling to the community: 'you are a temple of God, and God's Spirit lives in you.' The figural relocation of God's tabernacling presence into the church coheres strongly with the dwelling-among-them promise.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when the priests had come out of the holy place, that the cloud filled Yahweh’s house, so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house. Then Solomon said, “Yahweh has said that he would dwell in the thick darkness. I have surely built you a house of habitation, a place for you to dwell in forever.”
echoes.note: At Solomon's dedication the glory-cloud fills the house so the LORD dwells in it; Solomon builds a house for God to inhabit forever. Paul's claim that God's Spirit dwells in the temple-community figurally re-applies the indwelling glory of the Jerusalem temple. The temple-as-dwelling-of-God theology supplies coherent background.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's restoration promise, 'My dwelling place shall be with them... I will be their God and they shall be my people,' projects God's sanctuary into the eschatological community. Paul's church-as-temple indwelt by the Spirit realizes this promised dwelling-with-the-people, making the allusion coherent with Second-Temple temple-eschatology.

echoes.text: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
echoes.note: Paul's warrant 'for God's temple is holy' draws on the Levitical holiness principle ('You shall be holy, for I the LORD am holy') as applied to sanctuary space. The holiness predicate grounding the warning against defilement coheres with the temple's sanctity, though the link is conceptual and faint.

echoes.text: He said to me, Son of man, do you see what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel do commit here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? But you shall again see yet other great abominations.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's vision of abominations defiling the sanctuary, provoking God to depart and judge, parallels Paul's warning that whoever destroys/defiles God's temple, God will destroy. The threat that desecrating the holy place brings divine destruction supplies a thematic echo, marked low and contested.

pericopes.text: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone thinks that he is wise among you in this world, let him become a fool, that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, “He has taken the wise in their craftiness.” And again, “The Lord knows the reasoning of the wise, that it is worthless.”

echoes.text: He takes the wise in their own craftiness; the counsel of the cunning is carried headlong.
echoes.note: Paul cites 'it is written, He has taken the wise in their craftiness,' a near-verbatim quotation of Eliphaz's words in Job 5:13 (the only OT occurrence of this saying). The formula 'for it is written' marks it as explicit Scripture citation. Volume, distinctiveness, and the introductory formula make this a high-confidence quotation; notably Paul follows the Hebrew sense rather than the LXX rendering.

echoes.text: Yahweh knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile.
echoes.note: Paul's 'And again, The Lord knows the reasoning of the wise, that it is worthless' quotes Psalm 94:11 (LXX 93:11), with 'the wise' substituted for the psalm's 'man' to fit the wisdom argument. The chained 'and again' citation formula and close verbal correspondence make this a high-confidence quotation. The deliberate adaptation ('the wise' for 'man') is a known Pauline tailoring of the source.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”
echoes.note: Isaiah declares that the wisdom of the wise shall perish and the discernment of the discerning be hidden, the prophetic plank already cited at 1 Cor 1:19 and standing behind 'the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.' Its recurrence in the letter's wisdom polemic gives this echo coherence within 3:18-20, reinforcing the divine overturning of human wisdom.

echoes.text: The wise men are disappointed. They are dismayed and trapped. Behold, they have rejected Yahweh’s word. What kind of wisdom is in them?
echoes.note: Jeremiah taunts that the wise are put to shame, having rejected the LORD's word, so 'what wisdom is in them?' This coheres with Paul's call to become a fool to be wise and the futility of the wise, but the link is thematic and faint relative to the explicit Job and Psalm citations. Marked low and contested.

pericopes.text: Therefore let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. All are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Jeremiah forbids the wise, mighty, and rich to boast, allowing boasting only in knowing the LORD; Paul's 'let no one boast in men' applies this anti-boasting principle (already quoted at 1 Cor 1:31). Its recurrence in the letter and coherence with the wisdom-and-boasting theme support a medium echo, redirecting boasting from human teachers to God.

echoes.text: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: Paul's catalogue 'all things are yours... the world... things present, things to come' may evoke the creation mandate of dominion over all things now restored to those who belong to Christ. The link is to the figural inheritance/dominion theme rather than a verbal citation, so it is faint and contested.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: The psalm's 'you have put all things under his feet' undergirds the early Christian conviction that all things belong to those in Christ. Paul's 'all things are yours' may draw on this dominion-over-all-things theology, but the connection is diffuse and contested here, lacking verbal markers in this pericope.

pericopes.text: So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants, and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required of stewards, that they be found faithful. But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by man’s judgment. Yes, I don’t judge my own self. For I know nothing against myself. Yet I am not justified by this, but he who judges me is the Lord. Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and reveal the counsels of the hearts. Then each man will get his praise from God.

echoes.text: he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
echoes.note: Paul's claim that the Lord at his coming 'will bring to light the hidden things of darkness' echoes Daniel's praise that God 'reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.' The pairing of God revealing hidden things and darkness/light is verbally and conceptually close, and Daniel is a primary Second-Temple locus for divine disclosure of mysteries (mystērion), the very term Paul uses in v.1.

echoes.text: He uncovers deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shadow of death.
echoes.note: 'He uncovers deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shadow of death' supplies the same image Paul deploys: God exposing what is concealed in darkness. The verbal coherence (darkness brought to light) supports an echo, though the motif is widespread enough to be one of several converging texts rather than a single quotation.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's conclusion that 'God will bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil' parallels Paul's eschatological judgment that discloses the heart's hidden counsels so each receives praise. The shared structure of a final divine assize over hidden things gives this echo coherence with Paul's argument against premature human judgment.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways' grounds Paul's insistence that the Lord—not the Corinthians—judges, weighing hidden motives and rendering each his due. The heart-searching God who recompenses by inward reality coheres tightly with v.5's revelation of the counsels of the hearts.

echoes.text: You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence.
echoes.note: 'You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your face' offers the secret-sins-exposed-to-divine-light motif underlying v.5. The echo is faint and one of a cluster, but it reinforces the heart-exposure theme; marked low for limited verbal volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar.
echoes.note: The psalm's God who searches and knows the psalmist, discerning his thoughts from afar, underlies Paul's confidence that the Lord alone reads the hidden counsels of the heart. A diffuse echo in the same heart-searching tradition as Jeremiah 17:10; low for lack of distinctive wording.

pericopes.text: Now these things, brothers, I have in a figure transferred to myself and Apollos for your sakes, that in us you might learn not to think beyond the things which are written, that none of you be puffed up against one another. For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Don't be wise in your own eyes' resonates with Paul's warning against being 'puffed up' beyond 'the things which are written.' The wisdom tradition's caution against self-inflated wisdom coheres with Paul's deflation of Corinthian boasting, though no verbal quotation is present.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's command not to glory in wisdom, might, or riches but only in the Lord stands behind Paul's challenge in v.7: 'What do you have that you didn't receive? Why do you boast?' Paul elsewhere quotes this Jeremiah passage in the same letter (1:31), strengthening recurrence; here the un-derivative boasting Paul attacks is precisely the self-glory Jeremiah forbids.

echoes.text: and lest you say in your heart, “My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth.” But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth; that he may establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers, as at this day.
echoes.note: Moses' warning that Israel must not say 'My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth,' but remember it is the Lord who gives the power, matches Paul's logic that everything is received, leaving no ground for boasting. The gift-not-achievement theme coheres closely with v.7.

echoes.text: But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.
echoes.note: David's prayer, 'all things come from you, and of your own have we given you,' captures the received-gift theology of v.7. A thematic echo of creaturely receipt undercutting self-glory; low because the connection is conceptual rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: You are already filled. You have already become rich. You have come to reign without us. Yes, and I wish that you did reign, that we also might reign with you. For, I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, last of all, like men sentenced to death. For we are made a spectacle to the world, both to angels and men. We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You have honor, but we have dishonor. Even to this present hour we hunger, thirst, are naked, are beaten, and have no certain dwelling place. We toil, working with our own hands. When people curse us, we bless. Being persecuted, we endure. Being defamed, we entreat. We are made as the filth of the world, the dirt wiped off by all, even until now.

echoes.text: Yes, for your sake we are killed all day long. We are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.
echoes.note: 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter' underlies Paul's depiction of the apostles displayed 'like men sentenced to death,' a spectacle suffering for the gospel. Paul cites this very psalm in Romans 8:36, evidencing recurrence and a settled reading of the righteous-as-condemned motif.

echoes.text: You have made us an off-scouring and refuse in the midst of the peoples.
echoes.note: 'You have made us an offscouring and refuse in the middle of the peoples' is verbally the closest OT analogue to Paul's 'we are made as the filth of the world, the dirt wiped off by all' (v.13). The rare offscouring/refuse imagery applied to a suffering people of God gives this high volume and coherence with Paul's catalogue of abasement.

echoes.text: I have also become a reproach to them. When they see me, they shake their head.
echoes.note: 'I have become a reproach to them; when they see me, they shake their head' matches the reviling and defaming the apostles endure (vv.12-13) as the righteous-sufferer treated with contempt. Coheres with the lament-psalm pattern of the persecuted righteous that shapes Paul's hardship list.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: The Servant 'despised and rejected by men,' held of no account, stands behind Paul's portrait of apostolic dishonor, weakness, and being scorned as fools and scum. The figural assimilation of apostles to the Suffering Servant pattern is coherent with Paul's Christ-conformed weakness, though no direct citation occurs.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The Servant who gives his back to the smiters and does not hide from shame and spitting parallels the beaten, reviled apostles who bless when cursed (vv.11-12). A faint figural echo within the Servant-suffering field; low for absence of distinctive shared wording.

echoes.text: I am like one who is a joke to his neighbor, I, who called on God, and he answered. The just, the blameless man is a joke.
echoes.note: Job, 'a laughingstock to his neighbor,' the just man mocked, anticipates the apostles made 'fools for Christ's sake' and a spectacle (vv.9-10). The Joban figure of the righteous turned object of derision coheres with Paul's reversal motif; faint and one of several wisdom echoes.

echoes.text: I am become a derision to all my people, and their song all the day.
echoes.note: 'I have become a derision to all my people, their song all day long' reinforces the reviled-and-defamed apostle of vv.12-13 within the same Lamentations matrix that supplies the offscouring image of v.13. Low individually but strengthens the Lamentations recurrence.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: Paul's 'we toil, working with our own hands' (v.12) faintly recalls the post-Edenic sentence of labor by the sweat of the brow. A diffuse echo of toil-as-creaturely-lot; low confidence and likely incidental.

pericopes.text: I don’t write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, yet not many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News. I beg you therefore, be imitators of me. Because of this I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, even as I teach everywhere in every assembly. Now some are puffed up, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing. And I will know, not the word of those who are puffed up, but the power. For the Kingdom of God is not in word, but in power. What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?

echoes.text: One who spares the rod hates his son, but one who loves him is careful to discipline him.
echoes.note: 'He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently' undergirds Paul's father-to-children stance closing with the choice 'Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love?' (vv.14-21). The paternal-discipline rod is drawn from Proverbs' instruction tradition and coheres with Paul calling them his beloved children.

echoes.text: Folly is bound up in the heart of a child: the rod of discipline drives it far from him.
echoes.note: 'The rod of discipline drives' folly far from a child reinforces the rod-of-paternal-correction image of v.21. A secondary wisdom echo alongside Proverbs 13:24; low because the single Proverbs locus already carries the allusion.

echoes.text: You shall break them with a rod of iron. You shall dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.”
echoes.note: The messianic 'rod of iron' with which the king may break the nations could color Paul's threatened apostolic 'rod' (v.21), framing his authority in quasi-royal terms. Contested and faint: the immediate background is paternal/wisdom discipline, not royal judgment, so the Psalm 2 register is a possible overtone at best.
echoes.lxxText: Thou shalt rule them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces as a potter's vessel.

echoes.text: He that loves his son will continue to lay stripes upon him, That he may have joy of him in the end.
echoes.note: 'He who loves his son will cause him to feel the rod often' restates the loving-father-with-rod ethic Paul invokes in v.21, evidencing the motif's currency in Second-Temple wisdom. Low and deuterocanonical, but it corroborates the availability of the disciplining-rod topos to Paul.

pericopes.text: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such sexual immorality as is not even named among the Gentiles, that one has his father’s wife. You are puffed up, and didn’t rather mourn, that he who had done this deed might be removed from among you.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife. It is your father’s nakedness.
echoes.note: Paul's phrase 'one has his father's wife' verbally echoes the Levitical incest prohibition 'the nakedness of thy father's wife thou shalt not uncover.' High Volume (distinctive 'father's wife' formula) and strong Coherence with Paul's argument that the church surpasses even Gentile mores; the Holiness Code is the controlling intertext for the whole chapter.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, nor the nakedness of your mother: she is your mother. You shall not uncover her nakedness.
echoes.note: The immediately preceding verse frames the offense as uncovering 'the nakedness of thy father,' the broader Holiness-Code matrix from which 18:8 follows. Coherent with Paul's sense of a violation more fundamental than a single statute, though 18:8 is the closer verbal match.

echoes.text: “‘The man who lies with his father’s wife has uncovered his father’s nakedness: both of them shall surely be put to death; their blood shall be upon them.
echoes.note: The capital-sanction parallel to 18:8: 'the man that lieth with his father's wife... both of them shall surely be put to death.' Its death penalty undergirds Paul's demand that the man 'be removed from among you,' linking the prohibition to communal expulsion. High Recurrence across Lev 18 and 20.

echoes.text: ‘Cursed is he who lies with his father’s wife, because he dishonors his father’s bed.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
echoes.note: 'Cursed be he that lieth with his father's wife' — the Deuteronomic curse-list naming the identical offense in nearly identical words. Strong Volume and Coherence; the covenantal curse motivates Paul's grief and call for removal rather than the Corinthians' boasting.

echoes.text: A man shall not take his father’s wife, and shall not uncover his father’s skirt.
echoes.note: 'A man shall not take his father's wife, nor discover his father's skirt' (LXX/Heb 23:1) restates the same prohibition in legislative form. Medium confidence because it overlaps Lev 18:8 and 27:20; included for Recurrence within the Torah's repeated condemnation of this exact union.

pericopes.text: For I most certainly, as being absent in body but present in spirit, have already, as though I were present, judged him who has done this thing. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, you being gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, are to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.”
echoes.note: 'Deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh' echoes the Lord handing Job over to the Satan 'in thine hand; but save his life' — affliction of the body permitted while the person is ultimately preserved. The structure of bodily harm under satanic agency with a saving limit gives moderate Coherence; the verbal link is conceptual rather than lexical.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.” So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The first delivery of Job's possessions into the Satan's power ('all that he hath is in thy power') reinforces the same handing-over schema. Low confidence and contested, included for Recurrence within the Job prologue's distinctive 'deliver to the Satan' motif behind Paul's formula.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
echoes.note: 'The destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved' may faintly resonate with the flesh/spirit duality of 'my spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh.' Faint and contested; offered for Availability within Israel's anthropology of mortal flesh versus enduring spirit.

pericopes.text: Your boasting is not good. Don’t you know that a little yeast leavens the whole lump? Purge out the old yeast, that you may be a new lump, even as you are unleavened. For indeed Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old yeast, neither with the yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

echoes.text: “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.
echoes.note: 'A little yeast leavens the whole lump... purge out the old yeast' draws directly on the Passover command to 'put away leaven out of your houses,' on pain of being 'cut off from Israel.' High Volume and Coherence: Paul reads the literal de-leavening as figural for purging the immoral man, and the cutting-off sanction matches 5:13.

echoes.text: There shall be no yeast found in your houses for seven days, for whoever eats that which is leavened, that soul shall be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he be a foreigner, or one who is born in the land.
echoes.note: 'Seven days shall there be no leaven found in your houses' supplies the totality of leaven-removal behind 'leavens the whole lump' and 'purge out the old yeast.' Strong Recurrence within the Passover legislation that controls the pericope.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: 'Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed' figurally identifies Jesus with the paschal lamb 'roast with fire, and unleavened bread' eaten that night. High Volume and Coherence: the lamb's sacrifice is the ground for keeping the feast 'with the unleavened bread of sincerity,' a paradigmatic figural reading of Exodus 12.

echoes.text: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.
echoes.note: The command that 'the whole assembly of Israel shall kill it' (the lamb) at twilight underlies 'Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.' Coherent with Paul's communal frame; the slaying of the paschal victim is the figural type fulfilled.

echoes.text: Unleavened bread shall be eaten throughout the seven days; and no leavened bread shall be seen with you, neither shall yeast be seen with you, in all your borders.
echoes.note: 'Unleavened bread shall be eaten... neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters' parallels 'keep the feast... with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.' Strong Coherence: the Feast of Unleavened Bread is the explicit referent of Paul's 'let us keep the feast.'

echoes.text: You shall eat no leavened bread with it. You shall eat unleavened bread with it seven days, even the bread of affliction; for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste; that you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt all the days of your life.
echoes.note: 'Thou shalt eat no leavened bread with it; seven days... even the bread of affliction' provides the Deuteronomic form of the unleavened-bread feast Paul invokes. High Recurrence alongside Exodus 12-13; reinforces the festal command behind 5:8.

echoes.text: No yeast shall be seen with you in all your borders seven days; neither shall any of the flesh, which you sacrifice the first day at evening, remain all night until the morning.
echoes.note: 'There shall be no leaven seen with thee in all thy coast seven days' restates the total purge of leaven during the feast. Medium confidence because it duplicates Exod 13:7; included for Recurrence of the leaven-removal command.

echoes.text: You shall observe the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib (for in it you came out of Egypt), and no one shall appear before me empty.
echoes.note: 'Thou shalt keep the feast of unleavened bread... as I commanded thee' is a further iteration of the festal command Paul reworks in 'let us keep the feast.' Low confidence, offered for Availability and Recurrence within the Pentateuch's repeated feast legislation.

pericopes.text: I wrote to you in my letter to have no company with sexual sinners; yet not at all meaning with the sexual sinners of this world, or with the covetous and extortionists, or with idolaters; for then you would have to leave the world. But as it is, I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother who is a sexual sinner, or covetous, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or an extortionist. Don’t even eat with such a person. For what have I to do with also judging those who are outside? Don’t you judge those who are within? But those who are outside, God judges. “Put away the wicked man from among yourselves.”

echoes.text: The hand of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: 'Put away the wicked man from among yourselves' quotes the Deuteronomic expulsion formula 'so thou shalt put the evil away from among you,' here closing the idolatry/false-witness statute.
