Highest Volume in the chapter (verbatim LXX clause) and capstone Coherence: the literal de-leavening of 5:7 is realized as covenantal purging of the offender.

echoes.text: then you shall do to him as he had thought to do to his brother. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: 'So shalt thou put the evil away from among you' recurs in the law of the false witness, one of several Deuteronomic occurrences of the formula Paul cites. Medium confidence as a parallel source for the same refrain; strong Recurrence supports its availability behind 5:13.

echoes.text: then they shall bring out the young lady to the door of her father’s house, and the men of her city shall stone her to death with stones, because she has done folly in Israel, to play the prostitute in her father’s house. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: 'So shalt thou put evil away from among you' concludes the sexual-purity statute on a bride found unchaste — thematically apt since Paul applies the formula to a sexual offender. Coherent pairing of the expulsion refrain with sexual sin strengthens the link.

echoes.text: then you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and you shall stone them to death with stones; the lady, because she didn’t cry, being in the city; and the man, because he has humbled his neighbor’s wife. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: The same 'put away evil from among you' caps the adultery law of vv.23-24, another sexual-sin instance of the refrain. Low confidence given heavy overlap with the other occurrences; listed for Recurrence.

echoes.text: If a man is found stealing any of his brothers of the children of Israel, and he deals with him as a slave, or sells him; then that thief shall die. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: 'So shalt thou put evil away from among you,' closing the law against man-stealing, is a further occurrence of the formula Paul draws on. Low confidence; included to document the full Recurrence pattern across Deuteronomy that establishes 5:13 as a stock covenantal citation.

echoes.text: That prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to draw you aside out of the way which Yahweh your God commanded you to walk in. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: 'So shalt thou put the evil away from the midst of thee,' closing the law against the idolatrous prophet, is especially apt since Paul's vice-list in 5:10-11 leads with idolaters. The idolatry context gives this occurrence of the refrain heightened Coherence with Paul's argument.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: 'Not to associate... not even eat with such a person' faintly recalls the blessed man who walks 'not in the counsel of the ungodly' — separation from the wicked as the mark of the righteous community. Faint and contested; offered for the broad wisdom motif of avoiding fellowship with sinners.

echoes.text: He that touches pitch will be defiled; And he that has fellowship with a proud man will become like to him.
echoes.note: 'He that toucheth pitch shall be defiled therewith' expresses the Second-Temple wisdom logic that contact with the wicked contaminates, undergirding Paul's 'have no company' and the leaven imagery. Low confidence, contested; valid by Availability as a deuterocanonical analogue to the contagion of sin.

echoes.text: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”
echoes.note: 'Those who are outside, God judges' resonates with Abraham's 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?' — God as the universal judge over outsiders while the community judges its own. Faint, contested echo of the divine-judge motif.

pericopes.text: Dare any of you, having a matter against his neighbor, go to law before the unrighteous, and not before the saints? Don’t you know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Don’t you know that we will judge angels? How much more, things that pertain to this life? If then, you have to judge things pertaining to this life, do you set them to judge who are of no account in the assembly? I say this to move you to shame. Isn’t there even one wise man among you who would be able to decide between his brothers? But brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers! Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you, that you have lawsuits one with another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? No, but you yourselves do wrong, and defraud, and that against your brothers.

echoes.text: until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.
echoes.note: Paul's rhetorical 'the saints will judge the world' draws directly on the eschatological assize of Dan 7:22, where judgment is given to 'the saints of the Most High' who then possess the kingdom. Volume is high (the distinctive pairing of holy ones + judgment + world dominion), and the theme coheres with Paul's argument that believers should not need pagan courts now since they will judge the cosmos. Availability is secure as a canonical apocalyptic source.

echoes.text: They will judge nations, and have dominion over peoples; And the Lord will reign over them for evermore.
echoes.note: 'They will judge nations and rule over peoples' provides a close Second-Temple parallel to the saints judging the world (v.2), framing the righteous as future judges/rulers in the age to come. Recurrence of this motif across Daniel, Wisdom, and 1 Enoch strengthens its availability, though Paul's wording is closer to Daniel; Wisdom supplies the wider tradition.

echoes.text: Let the saints rejoice in honor. Let them sing for joy on their beds. May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a two-edged sword in their hand; To execute vengeance on the nations, and punishments on the peoples; To bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron; to execute on them the written judgment. All his saints have this honor. Praise Yah!
echoes.note: The saints (hasidim) executing the written judgment upon the nations supplies a faint coherent backdrop to believers judging the world. Volume is low and verbal links are absent, but the motif of the holy ones as agents of eschatological judgment recurs in the same stream Paul taps.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The pseudepigraphal tradition of the holy ones gathered to enact judgment, and of judgment falling even upon angelic Watchers (1 En 10-16), undergirds Paul's startling claim that 'we will judge angels' (v.3). Cited only because the angel-judgment motif is otherwise unattested in the canonical OT and Availability rests on this Second-Temple stream.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD' coheres tightly with Paul's 'Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?' (v.7), counseling the renunciation of self-vindication. The wisdom ethic of leaving redress to God, paired with the righteous-sufferer posture, gives medium volume coherence.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me' parallels Paul's preference to suffer wrong rather than retaliate through litigation. A faint, coherent wisdom echo within the same proverbial cluster as 20:22.

pericopes.text: Or don’t you know that the unrighteous will not inherit the Kingdom of God? Don’t be deceived. Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor male prostitutes, nor homosexuals, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor extortionists, will inherit the Kingdom of God. Such were some of you, but you were washed. But you were sanctified. But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not lie with a man, as with a woman. That is detestable.
echoes.note: The vice list's prohibition of men lying with men (arsenokoitai, v.9) is widely understood to be coined from the LXX of Lev 18:22 (meta arsenos ou koimethese koiten gynaikos). High volume via the rare compound term and strong coherence with the Holiness Code's catalog of exclusionary sins.

echoes.text: “‘If a man lies with a male, as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination: they shall surely be put to death; their blood shall be upon them.
echoes.note: Lev 20:13 repeats the same LXX phrase (arsenos koiten gynaikos) and adds the death penalty, reinforcing the lexical derivation of arsenokoitai and the kingdom-exclusion logic. Recurrence across both Holiness-Code chapters strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: There shall be no prostitute of the daughters of Israel, neither shall there be a sodomite of the sons of Israel. You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute, or the wages of a male prostitute, into the house of Yahweh your God for any vow; for both of these are an abomination to Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: The prohibition of the cult prostitute (qadesh/qedeshah) and the refusal of the 'wage of a dog' coheres with Paul's pairing of malakoi/pornoi and idolaters in a vice list, since cultic prostitution joined sexual sin to idolatry. Medium volume; thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: The inclusion of adulterers (moichoi) and thieves in the catalog echoes the Decalogue's prohibitions of adultery and theft, the foundational covenant ethic underlying Paul's roster of those excluded from the kingdom. Coherent but diffuse, as vice lists conventionally absorb Decalogue categories.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.
echoes.note: 'You were washed' (v.11) resonates with Ezekiel's new-covenant promise, 'I will sprinkle clean water on you and you shall be clean,' joined there to sanctification and the gift of the Spirit, exactly the triad Paul deploys (washed, sanctified, justified, in the Spirit). Coherence is strong; the cleansing-plus-Spirit pairing supports the allusion.

echoes.text: Wash yourselves, make yourself clean. Put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes. Cease to do evil.
echoes.note: 'Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your deeds' offers a prophetic moral-cleansing backdrop to 'you were washed' following a vice list. Faint and contested against the stronger ritual/Spirit cleansing of Ezek 36:25.

pericopes.text: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are expedient. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything. “Foods for the belly, and the belly for foods,” but God will bring to nothing both it and them. But the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body. Now God raised up the Lord, and will also raise us up by his power.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'God raised up the Lord and will also raise us up by his power' (v.14) draws on the canonical hope of bodily resurrection first explicit in Dan 12:2 ('many who sleep in the dust shall awake'). Coherent with Paul's bodily theology against the slogan that the belly/body is destined for nothing; medium volume as the foundational OT resurrection text.

echoes.text: And being come near to death he said thus: It is good to die at the hands of men and look for the hopes which are given by God, that we shall be raised up again by him; for as for you, you shall have no resurrection to life.
echoes.note: The martyrs' confidence of being raised up by God supplies a Second-Temple parallel to Paul's resurrection assurance in v.14, attesting the availability of bodily-resurrection hope. Faint and supplementary to Dan 12:2.

pericopes.text: Don’t you know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them members of a prostitute? May it never be! Or don’t you know that he who is joined to a prostitute is one body? For, “The two”, he says, “will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: Paul explicitly cites Gen 2:24 with a citation formula ('For, he says, the two will become one flesh', v.16) to prove that union with a prostitute makes one body with her. High volume and an unambiguous LXX quotation; the creation text is wrenched into an argument it never anticipated, a paradigmatic Pauline use.

echoes.text: You shall fear Yahweh your God; you shall serve him; and you shall cling to him, and you shall swear by his name.
echoes.note: 'He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit' (v.17) plays on the LXX language of cleaving/being joined (kollao) to the LORD found in Deut 10:20 ('him shall you cleave to'), the covenantal counter-image to illicit bodily union. Coherence is strong given the deliberate contrast Paul builds between the two kinds of joining.

echoes.text: to love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him; for he is your life, and the length of your days; that you may dwell in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.
echoes.note: Cleaving to the LORD as the source of life (LXX kollasthai) recurs here, reinforcing the covenantal 'joined to the Lord' motif of v.17. A faint recurrence within the Deuteronomic cleaving stream rather than a discrete source.

pericopes.text: Flee sexual immorality! “Every sin that a man does is outside the body,” but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body. Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit which is in you, which you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.

echoes.text: She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.
echoes.note: 'Flee sexual immorality!' (v.18) evokes the paradigm of Joseph who literally fled and left his garment to escape Potiphar's wife, the canonical exemplar of fleeing porneia. Coherent and recognized in Jewish moral tradition (cf. Wisdom-Joseph paraenesis); medium volume by motif.

echoes.text: Remove your way far from her. Don’t come near the door of her house,
echoes.note: 'Keep your way far from her, do not go near the door of her house' supplies the wisdom counsel to flee the adulteress lying behind Paul's imperative to flee porneia. Faint verbal contact but coherent within the same paraenetic tradition.

echoes.text: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.
echoes.note: 'Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit' (v.19) figurally transfers the sanctuary motif, 'let them make me a sanctuary that I may dwell among them,' onto the believer's body as God's indwelt dwelling. The Spirit-indwelling makes the body holy space; medium volume as a figural reapplication of tabernacle theology.

echoes.text: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: 'I will make my dwelling among you... and walk among you' undergirds the temple-of-the-Spirit image, the covenant promise of God's indwelling presence now located in the believer's body. A coherent but diffuse echo supplementing the Exodus sanctuary text.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: 'My dwelling place shall be with them' continues the indwelling-sanctuary stream Paul figurally applies to the Spirit-filled body in v.19. Faint and recurrent rather than a single discrete source.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, “You were sold for nothing; and you shall be redeemed without money.”
echoes.note: 'You were bought with a price' (v.20) evokes the redemption language of Isa 52:3 ('you were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money'), reframing the believer as God's purchased possession who is no longer his own. Coherent with the surrounding new-exodus redemption motif; medium volume by theme.

echoes.text: If there are yet many years, according to them he shall give back the price of his redemption out of the money that he was bought for. If there remain but a few years to the year of jubilee, then he shall reckon with him; according to his years of service he shall give back the price of his redemption.
echoes.note: The jubilee redemption-price legislation, where a person is bought back according to a reckoned price, supplies the legal-economic backdrop for 'bought with a price' and belonging now to another master. Faint and contested against the prophetic redemption of Isa 52:3.

echoes.text: everyone who is called by my name, and whom I have created for my glory, whom I have formed, yes, whom I have made.’”
echoes.note: 'Whom I created for my glory' provides a faint backdrop to 'glorify God in your body' (v.20), the redeemed belonging to God for his glory. Low volume; offered as a possible coherent echo of the purpose-of-redemption theme.

pericopes.text: Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But, because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render to his wife the affection owed her, and likewise also the wife to her husband. The wife doesn’t have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife. Don’t deprive one another, unless it is by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, and may be together again, that Satan doesn’t tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But this I say by way of concession, not of commandment. Yet I wish that all men were like me. However each man has his own gift from God, one of this kind, and another of that kind.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: The mutual conjugal claim Paul articulates (neither spouse has authority over their own body) presupposes the one-flesh union of Gen 2:24, the foundational text Paul cites explicitly in the prior pericope (6:16). Coherence is high because Paul's entire marriage theology in this letter rests on the Genesis joining; the body-language of belonging to one another extends that figure. Volume is moderate since no words are shared, but recurrence in the immediate context strengthens it.

echoes.text: If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, and her marital rights.
echoes.note: Paul's insistence that the husband render to the wife her due 'affection' (conjugal duty) and that neither defraud the other echoes the Torah's protection of a wife's marital rights in Ex 21:10, where a man may not diminish her food, clothing, or conjugal rights (onah). Second-Temple and rabbinic readings made onah a fixed marital obligation; coherence with Paul's reciprocal duty-language is strong. Volume is low (no quotation) but the legal concept is distinctive and available.

echoes.text: He said to the people, “Be ready by the third day. Don’t have sexual relations with a woman.”
echoes.note: Paul permits temporary abstinence 'by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to prayer'—the only sanctioned reason to interrupt conjugal duty—which mirrors Moses' command before Sinai to abstain from sexual relations to be ready to meet God ('do not go near a woman'). The pattern of cultic abstinence preparatory to encounter with God is the available precedent. Coherence is high; volume rests on the shared logic rather than wording, so confidence is medium.

echoes.text: Gather the people. Sanctify the assembly. Assemble the elders. Gather the children, and those who nurse from breasts. Let the bridegroom go out of his room, and the bride out of her room.
echoes.note: The pairing of communal fasting/prayer with the temporary suspension of marital intimacy faintly recalls Joel's summons in which even bride and bridegroom leave their chamber for the solemn assembly. The link is thematic (devotion overriding the marriage bed for a set time) rather than verbal. Contested and faint; the cultic-abstinence motif may equally derive from Ex 19.

echoes.text: Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Does Job fear God for nothing? Haven’t you made a hedge around him, and around his house, and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don’t stretch out your […]
echoes.note: Paul warns that prolonged abstinence may let Satan tempt them 'because of your lack of self-control,' invoking the Adversary as a tester of human fidelity—the role the satan plays in Job 1-2. Availability is secure (the satan as tester is a Second-Temple commonplace). Volume is low and the figure is generic, so the echo is faint and contested.

pericopes.text: But I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain even as I am. But if they don’t have self-control, let them marry. For it’s better to marry than to burn.

echoes.text: Can a man scoop fire into his lap, and his clothes not be burned? Or can one walk on hot coals, and his feet not be scorched?
echoes.note: Paul's maxim 'better to marry than to burn' uses the fire-of-desire image that Proverbs deploys for illicit passion ('Can a man carry fire in his bosom and his clothes not be burned?'). The metaphor of sexual desire as a consuming fire is the available sapiential trope. Volume is low (a single shared image, not a citation), and Paul's turn is positive (marriage as remedy), so the echo is faint and contested.

echoes.text: Two sorts of men multiply sins, And the third will bring wrath: A hot mind, as a burning fire, will not be quenched till it be consumed: A fornicator in the body of his flesh will never cease till he has burned out the fire. All bread is sweet to a fornicator: He will not leave off till he die.
echoes.note: Ben Sira describes the man of burning lust (the 'hot soul' kindled like a fire) who will not stop till consumed, the deuterocanonical development of desire-as-fire that lies behind Paul's 'better to marry than to burn.' Availability and coherence with Paul's self-control theme are good; volume is low. Contested as a faint conceptual echo rather than allusion.

pericopes.text: But to the married I command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife not leave her husband (but if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or else be reconciled to her husband), and that the husband not leave his wife.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: Paul's dominical prohibition of divorce ('the wife not leave her husband... the husband not leave his wife') is grounded in the one-flesh permanence of Gen 2:24, the very text Jesus cited against divorce in the tradition Paul invokes ('not I, but the Lord'). Coherence is high; the indissolubility logic flows directly from the Genesis joining. Volume is conceptual rather than verbal, hence medium.

echoes.text: For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him who covers his garment with violence!” says Yahweh of Armies. “Therefore take heed to your spirit, that you don’t deal treacherously.
echoes.note: Paul's command that spouses not separate echoes the prophetic denunciation of divorce in Mal 2:16 ('I hate divorce, says the Lord'), the strongest OT statement against putting away one's wife. Coherence is high with Paul's appeal to the Lord's authority on marital permanence. Volume is thematic, not lexical; the prophetic source is available and distinctive, so confidence is medium.

pericopes.text: But to the rest I—not the Lord—say, if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she is content to live with him, let him not leave her. The woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he is content to live with her, let her not leave her husband. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. Yet if the unbeliever departs, let there be separation. The brother or the sister is not under bondage in such cases, but God has called us in peace. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

echoes.text: Now when these things were done, the princes drew near to me, saying, “The people of Israel, and the priests and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands, following their abominations, even those of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. For they have taken of their daughters for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy seed have […]
echoes.note: Paul reverses the logic of Ezra-Nehemiah's covenant purity crisis: there the 'holy seed' was defiled by mixed marriage and foreign wives had to be put away, whereas Paul declares the unbelieving spouse sanctified and the children holy, so the believer must not separate. The figural inversion presupposes the Ezra paradigm of holiness-by-contagion through marriage. Coherence and availability are high; this is a deliberate counter-reading, hence figural.

echoes.text: Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.
echoes.note: Paul's concern that the children of a mixed marriage are 'holy' rather than 'unclean' resonates with Mal 2:15, where God seeks 'godly offspring' from the marriage union as the reason for fidelity. The shared interest in the covenantal status of children of marriage gives coherence; volume is low and the connection conceptual. Contested as a faint background echo.

echoes.text: “Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Ask now the priests concerning the law, saying, ‘If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment, and with his fold touches bread, stew, wine, oil, or any food, will it become holy?’” The priests answered, “No.” Then Haggai said, “If one who is unclean by reason of a dead body touch any of these, will it be unclean?” The priests answered, “It will be unclean.”
echoes.note: Paul's sanctification language assumes holiness is communicable through the marriage bond (the unbelieving spouse is made holy, the children holy), inverting the priestly ruling in Hag 2:11-13 that uncleanness spreads by contact but holiness does not. The cultic transmission-of-holiness/defilement framework is the available conceptual matrix. Volume is low and the link contested.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, put on your strength, Zion; put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.
echoes.note: The contrast of 'unclean' versus 'holy' applied to the household faintly recalls the holiness/uncleanness boundary language of Isa 52:1 ('no more shall the uncircumcised and the unclean enter you'). The link is lexical-thematic only (clean/unclean, holy) and very faint; contested.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: Paul's closing principle that 'God has called us in peace' (permitting separation when the unbeliever departs) echoes the sapiential-psalmic imperative to 'seek peace and pursue it.' The peace motif is generic and available; volume is low. Contested and faint.

pericopes.text: Only, as the Lord has distributed to each man, as God has called each, so let him walk. So I command in all the assemblies. Was anyone called having been circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Has anyone been called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God. Let each man stay in that calling in which he was called. Were you called being a bondservant? Don’t let that bother you, but if you get an opportunity to become free, use it. For he who was called in the Lord being a bondservant is the Lord’s free man. Likewise he who was called being free is Christ’s bondservant. You were bought with a price. Don’t become bondservants of men. Brothers, let each man, in whatever condition he was called, stay in that condition with God.

echoes.text: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.
echoes.note: Paul's relativizing of physical circumcision ('Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God') stands in the prophetic-Deuteronomic tradition that subordinates the bodily rite to the 'circumcision of the heart' and obedience (Deut 10:16). Coherence is high: Paul keeps the command-keeping while voiding the flesh-mark, exactly the Deuteronomic move. Volume is conceptual; the source is distinctive and available.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: Paul's claim that what counts is keeping God's commandments, not the circumcised flesh, draws on Deut 30:6, where the Lord himself circumcises the heart so that Israel will love and obey him—internalized obedience displacing the external sign. Coherence with Paul's argument is strong. Recurrence of the heart-circumcision motif across Deuteronomy and the prophets reinforces availability; medium confidence.

echoes.text: Circumcise yourselves to Yahweh, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's command to 'circumcise yourselves to the Lord, remove the foreskin of your hearts' is part of the prophetic tradition that makes literal circumcision insufficient apart from obedience—the background to Paul's 'circumcision is nothing.' Coherence and availability are high; the link is thematic rather than verbal, hence allusion at medium confidence.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will punish all those who are circumcised in uncircumcision: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that have the corners of their hair cut off, who dwell in the wilderness; for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.
echoes.note: Jer 9:25-26 announces judgment on those 'circumcised yet uncircumcised' in heart, lumping circumcised Israel with the uncircumcised nations—dissolving the very distinction Paul flattens ('neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts'). The distinctive prophetic leveling of the two states is the available precedent. Coherence is high; volume conceptual, medium confidence.

echoes.text: This is the end of the matter. All has been heard. Fear God, and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.
echoes.note: Paul's summation that 'the keeping of the commandments of God' is the one thing that counts closely matches Qoheleth's epilogue: 'Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.' The phrase 'keep the commandments' is shared and the sapiential reduction-to-essentials coheres with Paul's move. Volume is moderate but the phrase is common in the LXX, so the echo is real yet contested.

echoes.text: For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be sold as slaves.
echoes.note: Paul's 'You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men' rests on the Levitical principle that Israelites are God's own servants ('they are my servants, whom I brought out of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves'), so their ultimate ownership belongs to God, not human masters. Coherence with Paul's slave/free argument is strong. The redemption-from-slavery theology is distinctive and available; medium confidence.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, “You were sold for nothing; and you shall be redeemed without money.”
echoes.note: Paul's redemption formula 'you were bought with a price' inverts Isa 52:3, 'you were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money'—the prophetic image of God reclaiming his enslaved people. The buying/redeeming-from-bondage motif coheres exactly with Paul's exhortation to slaves and freedmen. Volume is conceptual; the distinctive redemption language makes it a plausible allusion at medium confidence.

echoes.text: For to me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: The premise that the redeemed belong to God and therefore should not become slaves of men ('to me the people of Israel are servants') reinforces 7:23 and is part of the same Jubilee slave-law complex as Lev 25:42. Listed as a faint, recurring background echo to the bought-with-a-price logic; contested.

pericopes.text: Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be trustworthy. I think that it is good therefore, because of the distress that is on us, that it is good for a man to be as he is. Are you bound to a wife? Don’t seek to be freed. Are you free from a wife? Don’t seek a wife. But if you marry, you have not sinned. If a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such will have oppression in the flesh, and I want to spare you. But I say this, brothers: the time is short, that from now on, both those who have wives may be as though they had none; and those who weep, as though they didn’t weep; and those who rejoice, as though they didn’t rejoice; and those who buy, as though they didn’t possess; and those who use the world, as not using it to the fullest. For the mode of this world passes away.

echoes.text: One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.
echoes.note: Paul's declaration that 'the mode of this world passes away' and his counsel to hold possessions loosely echo Qoheleth's vision of generations and the world in ceaseless passing under the sun, where buying, weeping, and rejoicing are all hevel. Coherence is high: the 'as though not' detachment from marriage, mourning, joy, and commerce mirrors Ecclesiastes' relativizing of all worldly engagements. Volume is thematic; medium.

echoes.text: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: Paul's claim that 'the present form of this world is passing away' stands in the prophetic tradition of Isa 40:6-8, where 'all flesh is grass' and the world's glory withers while God's word stands—the contrast of transient world and enduring divine order that grounds Paul's eschatological detachment. Coherence and availability are high. Volume conceptual; medium confidence.

echoes.text: Behold, you have made my days hand breadths. My lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely every man stands as a breath.” Selah. “Surely every man walks like a shadow. Surely they busy themselves in vain. He heaps up, and doesn’t know who shall gather.
echoes.note: Paul's 'those who buy as though they did not possess' and the fleeting 'form of this world' closely match Ps 39:6: 'man goes about as a shadow; he heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather it.' The shared image of buying/possessing as vain because life and world are transient is distinctive. Coherence with Paul's 'as though not' is strong; medium.

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.
echoes.note: Paul's sense that 'the time has grown short' and 'distress is upon us' echoes the prophetic announcement that the Day of the Lord is near and at hand (Zeph 1:7, 14), with its imminence relativizing ordinary life and commerce. Availability is secure; volume is low and the imminence motif is widespread, so the specific echo is contested.

echoes.text: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
echoes.note: Paul's catalogue 'those who weep as though they did not weep, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice' faintly recalls Qoheleth's 'a time to weep and a time to laugh,' the sapiential relativizing of the emotional seasons of life. The link is thematic and the wording diverges; faint and contested.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: Paul's reference to the present 'distress' and the foreshortened time may draw on Danielic expectation of a time of unparalleled distress before the end (Dan 12:1) and the apocalyptic notion of an appointed time cut short. Availability is good in a Second-Temple frame; volume is low and generic, so this is a faint contested echo.

pericopes.text: But I desire to have you to be free from cares. He who is unmarried is concerned for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but he who is married is concerned about the things of the world, how he may please his wife. There is also a difference between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman cares about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. But she who is married cares about the things of the world—how she may please her husband. This I say for your own profit; not that I may ensnare you, but for that which is appropriate, and that you may attend to the Lord without distraction.

echoes.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
echoes.note: Paul's wish that believers be 'free from cares' (anxieties) and devoted to the Lord faintly echoes the psalmic counsel to 'cast your burden on the Lord.' The anxiety/care language is generic, and Paul's point (undistracted devotion) is his own; the echo is faint and contested.

echoes.text: One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after, that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.
echoes.note: Paul's ideal of attending to the Lord 'without distraction'—the unmarried devoted to the things of the Lord—resonates with the psalmist's single desire 'to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to gaze upon his beauty.' The undivided-devotion motif coheres; volume is low and conceptual. Contested.

pericopes.text: But if any man thinks that he is behaving inappropriately toward his virgin, if she is past the flower of her age, and if need so requires, let him do what he desires. He doesn’t sin. Let them marry. But he who stands steadfast in his heart, having no necessity, but has power over his own heart, to keep his own virgin, does well. So then both he who gives his own virgin in marriage does well, and he who doesn’t give her in marriage does better.

echoes.text: A daughter is a secret cause of wakefulness to a father; And the care for her puts away sleep; In her youth, lest she pass the flower of her age; And when she is married, lest she should be hated: In her virginity, lest she should be defiled And be with child in her father’s house; And when she has a husband, lest she should transgress; And when she is married, lest she should be barren. Keep a strict watch over a headstrong daughter, Lest she make you a […]
echoes.note: Paul's scenario of a man anxious about his virgin (daughter or betrothed) 'past the flower of her age' and deciding whether to give her in marriage closely matches Ben Sira's portrait of the father's sleepless anxiety over an unmarried daughter, lest she pass her prime and not be given away. The shared cultural concern—a guardian's responsibility over a maturing virgin's marriage—is distinctive and available. Coherence is strong; medium confidence.

pericopes.text: A wife is bound by law for as long as her husband lives; but if the husband is dead, she is free to be married to whomever she desires, only in the Lord. But she is happier if she stays as she is, in my judgment, and I think that I also have God’s Spirit.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: Paul's rule that 'a wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives' but is freed at his death restates the lifelong one-flesh bond of Gen 2:24 in legal terms. Coherence with Paul's recurrent use of the Genesis joining throughout the chapter is good; volume here is conceptual and the legal formulation generic, so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: “But the vow of a widow, or of her who is divorced, everything with which she has bound her soul, shall stand against her.
echoes.note: Paul's statement that a widow 'is free to be married to whomever she desires' parallels the Torah's treatment of the widow as released from the binding obligations she bore while her husband lived (Num 30:9, where a widow's vow stands precisely because she is no longer under a husband). The shared legal logic of the husband's death releasing the wife from binding is the available background; faint and contested.

pericopes.text: Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, the same is known by him.

echoes.text: Moses said to Yahweh, “Behold, you tell me, ‘Bring up this people:’ and you haven’t let me know whom you will send with me. Yet you have said, ‘I know you by name, and you have also found favor in my sight.’
echoes.note: Paul's "if anyone loves God, the same is known by him" inverts the human-knows-God expectation toward God's prior knowing, echoing the LORD's word to Moses, "I know you by name." The motif of God's elective knowledge of a person is the Septuagintal idiom Paul draws on; the verbal link is the divine "knowing" of the favored one. Coherence is strong with Paul's wider theology of being foreknown.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “I will do this thing also that you have spoken; for you have found favor in my sight, and I know you by name.”
echoes.note: "You have found favor in my sight, and I know you by name" supplies the same pattern of God knowing the one who loves/serves him that Paul reuses to relativize human knowledge. Recurrence with Exod 33:12 strengthens the case for a Mosaic backdrop. Marked echo rather than quotation because Paul reworks it into a general maxim.

echoes.text: Yahweh is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him.
echoes.note: "The LORD is good... and he knows those who take refuge in him" parallels Paul's "is known by him," the divine knowing of those who love God. The thematic coherence is real but the volume is faint and the wording divergent. Offered as a plausible secondary resonance.

echoes.text: For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.
echoes.note: "The LORD knows the way of the righteous" is the wisdom-tradition counterpart to Paul's claim that the one who loves God is known by him. Faint volume; offered as a candidate for the OT idiom of God's saving knowledge of the righteous. Contested because no verbal contact beyond the verb "know."

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Jeremiah contrasts boasting in wisdom with knowing the LORD, exactly Paul's move against knowledge that "puffs up." Paul cites this passage explicitly at 1 Cor 1:31, making its availability and recurrence in this letter strong, so the contrast of human gnosis vs. knowing/being known by God plausibly stands behind 8:1-3 as well. Coherence with Paul's anti-boasting theme is high.

pericopes.text: Therefore concerning the eating of things sacrificed to idols, we know that no idol is anything in the world, and that there is no other God but one. For though there are things that are called “gods”, whether in the heavens or on earth; as there are many “gods” and many “lords”; yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we live through him.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: "There is no God but one" (v.4) and "to us there is one God" (v.6) directly rework the Shema, "the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Paul splits the one kyrios-theos confession into "one God, the Father" and "one Lord, Jesus Christ," a christological re-reading of the foundational monotheistic creed. High volume, high coherence, and the Shema's universal availability make this the controlling OT text of the pericope.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's command to love the LORD continues into Paul's framing, linking 8:3 ("if anyone loves God") to the one-God confession of 8:4-6. The pairing of loving God and confessing one God reproduces the Deuteronomic sequence. Marked as echo since v.5 is implied by Paul's use of the whole Shema unit.

echoes.text: It was shown to you so that you might know that Yahweh is God. There is no one else besides him.
echoes.note: "The LORD is God; there is no other besides him" is the explicit monotheistic formula Paul restates as "there is no other God but one." The negation "no other" matches closely. High volume and direct coherence with the chapter's argument that idols are nothing.

echoes.text: Know therefore this day, and lay it to your heart, that Yahweh himself is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath. There is no one else.
echoes.note: "The LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other" supplies both the exclusive monotheism and the heaven/earth merism Paul uses in v.5 ("in the heavens or on earth"). The spatial double phrase strengthens the link beyond generic monotheism. Coherence high.

echoes.text: This is what Yahweh, the King of Israel, and his Redeemer, Yahweh of Armies, says: “I am the first, and I am the last; and besides me there is no God.
echoes.note: "I am the first and the last; besides me there is no God" is a prime Deutero-Isaianic monotheistic declaration that Paul condenses into "no God but one." Isaiah 40-48 is Paul's deep well for monotheism-against-idolatry, supplying both the creed and the idol polemic of this chapter. High recurrence across Isaiah strengthens availability.

echoes.text: Don’t fear, neither be afraid. Haven’t I declared it to you long ago, and shown it? You are my witnesses. Is there a God besides me? Indeed, there is not. I don’t know any other Rock.”
echoes.note: "Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any" reinforces the exclusive monotheism Paul affirms in v.4. Part of the same oracle as 44:6, contributing to a cumulative Isaianic backdrop. Echo rather than quotation due to paraphrase.

echoes.text: I am Yahweh, and there is no one else. Besides me, there is no God. I will strengthen you, though you have not known me;
echoes.note: "I am the LORD, and there is no other; besides me there is no God" is among the clearest sources for Paul's "no God but one." The repeated Isaianic "none besides me" formula directly grounds the confession of v.4. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: The classic idol-polemic — idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands, that cannot see, speak, or act — underwrites Paul's "no idol is anything in the world." Psalm 115 reduces idols to nothing, exactly Paul's premise. The chapter's whole "food sacrificed to idols" logic rests on this conviction of idols' non-existence; high coherence and recurrence with the Isaianic polemic.

echoes.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they can’t speak. They have eyes, but they can’t see. They have ears, but they can’t hear; neither is there any breath in their mouths. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: A near-doublet of Psalm 115's idol satire (idols of silver and gold, work of human hands, mouths that cannot speak) reinforcing that idols are nothing. Recurrence with Ps 115 raises the volume of the idols-as-nothing theme behind v.4. Echo because Paul does not quote, only assumes the conclusion.

echoes.text: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's extended mockery of the idol-maker who fashions a god from a leftover log establishes that an idol "is nothing in the world," the very phrase-idea Paul uses in v.4. This is the locus classicus of idol-nothingness in the prophets and coheres tightly with Paul's argument. Allusion rather than quotation since Paul presupposes its conclusion.

echoes.text: For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it not move. They are like a palm tree, of turned work, and don’t speak: they must be carried, because they can’t go. Don’t be afraid of them; for they can’t do evil, neither is it in them to do good.”
echoes.note: "They are like a scarecrow... they cannot speak... neither is it in them to do good" — idols as powerless non-entities supports Paul's denial that any idol is anything. Part of the same prophetic idol-polemic stream as Isaiah 44 and Psalm 115. Faint-to-moderate volume; flagged as a recurring tradition.

echoes.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
echoes.note: "Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?" supplies Paul's distinctive pairing of one God with fatherhood and creation ("one God, the Father, of whom are all things") in v.6. The combination of "one Father" and "one God" who creates is rare and matches Paul's formulation closely. Coherence with the Shema-expansion is strong.

echoes.text: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.
echoes.note: "The LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords" stands behind Paul's concession in v.5 that there are "many gods and many lords" while affirming the one God and one Lord. The god-of-gods/lord-of-lords formula frames the polemic of relative vs. true deity. Echo, since Paul redeploys rather than cites it.

echoes.text: Give thanks to the God of gods; for his loving kindness endures forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords; for his loving kindness endures forever:
echoes.note: "Give thanks to the God of gods... the Lord of lords" parallels Paul's "many gods and many lords" / "one God... one Lord" antithesis in vv.5-6. Faint verbal contact through the gods/lords pairing; offered as a secondary resonance to Deut 10:17. Contested because the link is conceptual.

echoes.text: Yahweh will be King over all the earth. In that day Yahweh will be one, and his name one.
echoes.note: "The LORD will be king over all the earth; on that day the LORD will be one and his name one" is an eschatological echo of the Shema that, like Paul, projects the one-LORD confession onto all reality. Coheres with Paul's universalizing "of whom are all things" in v.6. Echo, marked for its Shema reworking.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: “The labor of Egypt, and the merchandise of Ethiopia, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you, and they shall be yours. They will go after you. They shall come over in chains; and they will bow down to you. They will make supplication to you: ‘Surely God is in you; and there is no one else. There is no other god.
echoes.note: "God is in you only, and there is no other, no god besides him" reinforces the exclusive-monotheism cluster behind v.4. Faint additional witness within Isaiah's monotheistic oracles. Low volume; included for the maximal sweep.

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]
echoes.note: Paul's "one Lord... through whom are all things" assigns to Christ the mediating role of Wisdom present at creation, by whom all things were made. The Wisdom-as-agent-of-creation tradition stands behind Paul's christological reworking of the Shema in v.6. Contested and faint, since the link is conceptual mediation rather than wording.

echoes.text: For verily all men by nature were but vain who had no perception of God, And from the good things that are seen they gained not power to know him that is, Neither by giving heed to the works did they recognize the architect; But either fire, or wind, or swift air, Or circling stars, or raging water, or luminaries of heaven, They thought to be gods that rule the world. And if it was through delight in their beauty that they took them to be gods, Let them […]
echoes.note: Hellenistic-Jewish polemic against those who, knowing the works of creation, fail to know the one God, paralleling Paul's contrast of true knowledge with idolatry. As Second-Temple idol-critique it is squarely available to Paul and his diaspora congregation. Echo of the deuterocanonical natural-theology argument behind vv.4-6.

echoes.text: For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication, And the invention of them the corruption of life: For neither were they from the beginning, neither will they be forever; For by the vaingloriousness of men they entered into the world, And therefore was a speedy end devised for them. For a father worn with untimely grief, Making an image of the child quickly taken away, Now honored him as a god which was then a dead man, And delivered to those […]
echoes.note: Wisdom traces idolatry to human invention and names idols empty objects of misplaced worship, supporting Paul's "no idol is anything." Available Second-Temple background to the chapter's premise. Faint volume; included to mark the recurring deuterocanonical idol-critique.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: Paul's "one God, the Father, of whom are all things" and "one Lord... through whom are all things" presuppose the creation account's one Creator of all. The creation-of-all-things motif grounds the monotheism of v.6. Faint, generic link, marked low.

pericopes.text: However, that knowledge isn’t in all men. But some, with consciousness of the idol until now, eat as of a thing sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. But food will not commend us to God. For neither, if we don’t eat, are we the worse; nor, if we eat, are we the better.

echoes.text: They shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to the goat idols, after which they play the prostitute. This shall be a statute forever to them throughout their generations.’
echoes.note: The prohibition of sacrifices to goat-demons frames the Israelite anxiety about idol-food that Paul's "weak" still feel as "consciousness of the idol." The defilement-by-idol-association logic of vv.7 draws on the Levitical sense that idolatrous sacrifice pollutes. Faint and conceptual; included for the defilement theme.

echoes.text: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
echoes.note: Daniel "resolved not to defile himself" with the king's food associated with idolatry, the paradigmatic Second-Temple case of conscience over defiling pagan food. This is the closest scriptural analogue to the "weak" conscience "defiled" by idol-food in v.7. Coherence high; the diaspora food-defilement motif is directly available.

echoes.text: You offer polluted bread on my altar. You say, ‘How have we polluted you?’ In that you say, ‘Yahweh’s table is contemptible.’
echoes.note: "Polluted food" offered on the altar links idol/improper offering with defilement, paralleling the "defiled" conscience over idol-food in v.7. Faint verbal contact through defiled food; offered as a secondary resonance to Daniel 1:8. Contested.

echoes.text: When I was carried away captive to Nineveh, all my kindred and my relatives ate of the bread of the Gentiles; but I kept myself from eating, because I remembered God with all my soul.
echoes.note: Tobit abstains from the food of the Gentiles, the same Second-Temple scruple over defilement by pagan food that animates the "weak" of v.7. Available deuterocanonical parallel to the conscience-and-food anxiety. Low volume, included for the maximal sweep.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: "The LORD looks on the heart" stands behind Paul's claim that "food will not commend us to God" (v.8) — outward consumption does not determine standing before God, who weighs the heart. Conceptual coherence with Paul's relativizing of food; faint wording. Contested.

echoes.text: I don’t rebuke you for your sacrifices. Your burnt offerings are continually before me. I have no need for a bull from your stall, nor male goats from your pens. For every animal of the forest is mine, and the livestock on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the mountains. The wild animals of the field are mine. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine, and all that is in it. Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of […]
echoes.note: God declares he has no need of sacrificial food ("I will not accept a bull... do I eat the flesh of bulls?"), grounding Paul's claim that food neither commends nor diminishes us before God (v.8). The prophetic critique that God is not won by eating coheres with Paul's argument. Faint volume; marked low.

pericopes.text: But be careful that by no means does this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to the weak. For if a man sees you who have knowledge sitting in an idol’s temple, won’t his conscience, if he is weak, be emboldened to eat things sacrificed to idols? And through your knowledge, he who is weak perishes, the brother for whose sake Christ died. Thus, sinning against the brothers, and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ. Therefore if food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more, that I don’t cause my brother to stumble.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: "You shall not put a stumbling block before the blind" is the foundational Torah text for Paul's warning that liberty must not become "a stumbling block to the weak" (v.9). The stumbling-block image and the protection of the vulnerable are taken straight from the Holiness Code. High coherence; the weak stand in for the blind as those liable to be tripped.

echoes.text: Son of man, these men have taken their idols into their heart, and put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face: should I be inquired of at all by them? Therefore speak to them, and tell them, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Every man of the house of Israel who takes his idols into his heart, and puts the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet; I Yahweh will answer him therein according to the multitude of his […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel condemns those who "set up their idols in their hearts and put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their faces," uniquely joining idols and stumbling block — exactly Paul's combination of idol-food and the stumbling block to the weak (vv.9-13). The conjunction of these two motifs is distinctive and strengthens the allusion. Coherence high.

echoes.text: They shall cast their silver in the streets, and their gold shall be as an unclean thing; their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of Yahweh: they shall not satisfy their souls, neither fill their bowels; because it has been the stumbling block of their iniquity.
echoes.note: Wealth become "the stumbling block of their iniquity" that defiles supplies the Ezekielian stumbling-block idiom Paul reuses in v.9. Recurrence with Ezek 14:3-4 supports an Ezekielian source for the metaphor. Faint independent volume; low.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
echoes.note: The LORD becomes "a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling" — the prophetic stumbling-stone tradition that informs Paul's stumbling-block language in vv.9,13. Conceptual, with the term shared; Paul applies it ethically to causing the weak to fall. Contested, low volume.

echoes.text: But you have turned aside out of the way. You have caused many to stumble in the law. You have corrupted the covenant of Levi,” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The priests have "caused many to stumble by your instruction," linking flawed teaching/knowledge to the stumbling of others, paralleling how the "knowledge" of the strong causes the weak to stumble (vv.10-11). Thematic coherence with Paul's critique of knowledge without love. Faint volume; low.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him. “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The command not to sin against your neighbor but to love him stands behind Paul's charge that wounding the weak brother's conscience is to "sin against the brothers" (v.12). Paul's love-of-neighbor logic governing this chapter draws on the Holiness Code's brother/neighbor ethic. Coherence strong with the love-builds-up theme of 8:1.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
echoes.note: "Am I my brother's keeper?" and the blood of the brother crying out frame Paul's insistence that the strong are responsible for the brother who perishes (v.11). The motif of culpability for a brother's destruction resonates faintly with Cain. Conceptual; included for the maximal sweep.

pericopes.text: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Haven’t I seen Jesus Christ, our Lord? Aren’t you my work in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, yet at least I am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

echoes.text: Wrap up the testimony. Seal the law among my disciples.
echoes.note: Paul calls the Corinthians 'the seal (sphragis) of my apostleship' (v.2), the validating proof of his commission. Isaiah's 'bind up the testimony, seal the teaching among my disciples' supplies a faint scriptural backdrop for a sealed witness that authenticates a prophetic commission. Volume is low and verbal contact slight; offered as a coherent echo within the prophetic-validation stream.

pericopes.text: My defense to those who examine me is this. Have we no right to eat and to drink? Have we no right to take along a wife who is a believer, even as the rest of the apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or have only Barnabas and I no right to not work? What soldier ever serves at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard, and doesn’t eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock, and doesn’t drink from the flock’s milk?

echoes.text: What man is there who has planted a vineyard, and has not used its fruit? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man use its fruit.
echoes.note: 'Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?' (v.7) draws on the Deuteronomic exemption, 'who has planted a vineyard and not enjoyed its fruit? Let him go home,' the principle that the laborer is entitled to the produce of his own work. Coherence is strong: Paul argues the worker rightly partakes of his labor's yield, and the vineyard image is the same. Medium volume by motif rather than wording.

echoes.text: Whoever tends the fig tree shall eat its fruit. He who looks after his master shall be honored.
echoes.note: 'Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored' coheres tightly with Paul's paired questions about the vinedresser eating the fruit and the shepherd drinking the milk (v.7): the one who works enjoys the produce. The proverb's join of tending-and-eating to honoring-a-master maps onto Paul's case for apostolic support. Medium volume by theme.

echoes.text: There will be plenty of goats’ milk for your food, for your family’s food, and for the nourishment of your servant girls.
echoes.note: 'There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household' supplies a wisdom backdrop to 'who feeds a flock and does not drink of the flock's milk?' (v.7). The flock-yields-milk-as-the-keeper's-food motif coheres with Paul's point, though verbal contact is faint; a low-volume echo within the same proverbial cluster as 27:18.

echoes.text: You will betroth a wife, and another man shall lie with her. You will build a house, and you won’t dwell in it. You will plant a vineyard, and not use its fruit.
echoes.note: 'You shall plant a vineyard but not enjoy its fruit' (a covenant curse) supplies the inverse of the natural expectation Paul invokes: that the planter ordinarily eats the fruit. A faint recurrence within the Deuteronomic vineyard-fruit stream, contested against the closer exemption of Deut 20:6.

echoes.text: “To the children of Levi, behold, I have given all the tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service which they serve, even the service of the Tent of Meeting.
echoes.note: The principle that the Levite is given the tithe 'in return for the service that they do' anticipates Paul's argument that the apostolic soldier/vinedresser/shepherd is entitled to support for his labor (vv.4-7). Faint at this point and developed more fully at vv.13-14; cited here for the laborer-deserves-his-keep coherence.

pericopes.text: Do I speak these things according to the ways of men? Or doesn’t the law also say the same thing? For it is written in the law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.” Is it for the oxen that God cares, or does he say it assuredly for our sake? Yes, it was written for our sake, because he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope should partake of his hope.

echoes.text: You shall not muzzle the ox when he treads out the grain.
echoes.note: Paul cites the law of Moses verbatim with a citation formula, 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain' (v.9, LXX ou phimoseis boun aloonta), as scriptural warrant for the worker's right to support. An unambiguous, high-volume quotation, then daringly reapplied ('Is it for the oxen that God cares, or for our sake?') to apostolic maintenance.

echoes.text: Come to her as one that plows and sows, And wait for her good fruits; For your toil will be little in the tillage of her, And you will eat of her fruits right soon.
echoes.note: 'Come to her as one who plows and sows, and wait for her good fruits' supplies a Second-Temple parallel to Paul's 'the plowman ought to plow in hope, and the thresher to thresh in hope of partaking' (v.10). The plow-sow-in-expectation-of-fruit topos and the very pairing of plowing with hopeful harvest cohere closely; medium volume, strengthening availability of the agricultural-hope figure.

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: The wisdom theme that the diligent worker rightly looks for his portion offers a faint backdrop to 'the thresher threshes in hope of partaking of the crop' (v.10). Low volume and no verbal contact; included as a coherent wisdom echo of the laborer's just expectation.

pericopes.text: If we sowed to you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we reap your fleshly things? If others partake of this right over you, don’t we yet more? Nevertheless we did not use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.

echoes.text: Fear the Lord, and glorify the priest; And give him his portion, even as it is commanded you; The first fruits, and the trespass offering, and the gift of the shoulders, And the sacrifice of sanctification, and the first fruits of holy things.
echoes.note: 'Honor the priest... give him his portion as you are commanded' parallels Paul's claim that those who sow spiritual things may reap material support (v.11) and have 'a right over you' (v.12). The reciprocity of material provision for sacred ministry coheres, though Paul develops the temple analogy explicitly only at v.13. Low volume, anticipatory echo.

pericopes.text: Don’t you know that those who serve around sacred things eat from the things of the temple, and those who wait on the altar have their portion with the altar? Even so the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Good News should live from the Good News.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Aaron, “Behold, I myself have given you the command of my wave offerings, even all the holy things of the children of Israel. I have given them to you by reason of the anointing, and to your sons, as a portion forever. This shall be yours of the most holy things from the fire: every offering of theirs, even every meal offering of theirs, and every sin offering of theirs, and every trespass offering of theirs, which they shall render to me, […]
echoes.note: 'Those who serve around sacred things eat from the things of the temple' (v.13) directly invokes the priestly-portion legislation of Num 18, where the LORD gives Aaron and his sons the offerings 'as a portion' to eat. High volume and strong coherence: Paul reasons from the temple economy to the gospel-worker's right to a living. The most secure source for the temple-eats-of-the-temple principle.

echoes.text: The priests the Levites, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion nor inheritance with Israel. They shall eat the offerings of Yahweh made by fire and his portion. They shall have no inheritance among their brothers. Yahweh is their inheritance, as he has spoken to them. This shall be the priests’ due from the people, from those who offer a sacrifice, whether it be ox or sheep, that they shall give to the priest the shoulder, the two cheeks, and the […]
echoes.note: 'The Levitical priests... shall eat the LORD's food offerings as their inheritance' supplies the parallel statute that the ministers of the altar live from the altar, exactly Paul's second clause, 'those who wait on the altar have their portion with the altar' (v.13). Recurrence of the priests-live-from-the-sanctuary rule across Numbers and Deuteronomy strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: That which is left of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten without yeast in a holy place. They shall eat it in the court of the Tent of Meeting. It shall not be baked with yeast. I have given it as their portion of my offerings made by fire. It is most holy, as the sin offering, and as the trespass offering. Every male among the children of Aaron shall eat of it, as their portion forever throughout your generations, from the offerings of […]
echoes.note: The Levitical rules assigning the priests their share of the grain, sin, and guilt offerings ('Aaron and his sons shall eat it... it is most holy') furnish the cultic detail behind 'eat from the things of the temple' and 'have their portion with the altar' (v.13). Medium volume; supplements the headline Num 18 / Deut 18 statutes with the offering-portion mechanics.

echoes.text: Every male among the priests may eat of it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy.
echoes.note: 'Every male among the priests may eat of it... it is most holy' (the guilt offering) reinforces the altar-servants-share-the-altar logic of v.13b. A faint recurrence within the Levitical priestly-portion stream, contested against the fuller Num 18 / Deut 18 basis.

echoes.text: You may eat it anywhere, you and your households, for it is your reward in return for your service in the Tent of Meeting.
echoes.note: 'You may eat it in any place... it is your reward for your service' tightly matches Paul's reasoning that ministerial service earns a livelihood (vv.13-14). A low-volume echo gathered with the broader Num 18 portion legislation.

pericopes.text: But I have used none of these things, and I don’t write these things that it may be done so in my case; for I would rather die, than that anyone should make my boasting void. For if I preach the Good News, I have nothing to boast about; for necessity is laid on me; but woe is to me, if I don’t preach the Good News. For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward. But if not of my own will, I have a stewardship entrusted to me. What then is my reward? That, when I preach the Good News, I may present the Good News of Christ without charge, so as not to abuse my authority in the Good News.

echoes.text: If I say, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with forbearing, and I can’t.
echoes.note: 'Necessity is laid on me; woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!' (v.16) closely echoes Jeremiah's compulsion: 'If I say I will not mention him... there is in my heart as it were a burning fire... and I cannot.' Both depict an inescapable divine constraint to proclaim despite the cost. Strong coherence with Paul's stewardship-not-of-his-own-will (v.17); high volume by the prophet-compelled-to-speak motif.

echoes.text: The lion has roared. Who will not fear? The Lord Yahweh has spoken. Who can but prophesy?
echoes.note: 'The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?' supplies the prophetic axiom of irresistible commission underlying Paul's 'necessity is laid on me' (v.16). Recurrence of the compelled-to-prophesy theme across Amos and Jeremiah strengthens availability; medium volume, contested against the closer inner-compulsion of Jer 20:9.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak.
echoes.note: The prophet sent under orders ('to all to whom I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak') offers a faint backdrop to Paul's 'stewardship entrusted to me... not of my own will' (v.17). Low volume; a coherent echo of the commissioned-and-bound prophet.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
echoes.note: 'Come, buy and eat... without money and without price' faintly resonates with Paul's resolve to 'present the gospel free of charge' (v.18). The free-offer-of-divine-bounty motif coheres, but verbal contact is slight; offered as a low-volume figural echo of grace given without cost.

pericopes.text: For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more. To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law; to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law. To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some. Now I do this for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high. Like as many were astonished at you (his appearance was marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men), so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they understand. Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of […]
