echoes.note: Paul's voluntary self-enslavement, 'though free from all, I made myself a servant to all, that I might win the more' (v.19), and his becoming weak with the weak to save some (v.22) faintly echo the Servant who makes himself nothing to bring many to righteousness ('by his knowledge shall the righteous one make many to be accounted righteous'). Low volume and no verbal citation; a coherent figural echo of the self-giving servant who saves the many.

pericopes.text: Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, that you may win. Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible. I therefore run like that, as not uncertainly. I fight like that, as not beating the air, but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.

echoes.text: When it is present, men imitate it; And they long after it when it is departed: And throughout all time it marcheth crowned in triumph, Victorious in the strife for the prizes that are undefiled.
echoes.note: 'It wears a crown and celebrates triumph, having won the contest for prizes that are undefiled' supplies the nearest Jewish parallel to Paul's athletic imagery of the race, the prize, and the 'imperishable crown' (vv.24-25). The contest-for-an-undefiled-crown topos coheres directly with Paul's incorruptible wreath versus the corruptible; medium volume, securing availability of the figure within Second-Temple thought.

echoes.text: Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.
echoes.note: 'The righteous... will receive a glorious crown and a beautiful diadem from the hand of the Lord' parallels Paul's imperishable victor's crown awarded to the disciplined runner (v.25). A coherent recurrence of the eschatological-crown-for-the-righteous motif, contested against the closer athletic-contest language of Wisdom 4:2.

echoes.text: I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happen to them all.
echoes.note: 'The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong' forms a wisdom counterpoint to Paul's exhortation that 'all run, but one receives the prize; so run that you may obtain' (v.24). Paul invokes the same race-and-prize frame Qoheleth relativizes; a faint, possibly deliberate echo with reversed force. Low volume.

echoes.text: She will give to your head a garland of grace. She will deliver a crown of splendor to you.”
echoes.note: Wisdom 'will place on your head a graceful garland; she will bestow on you a beautiful crown' offers a faint sapiential backdrop to the victor's crown of vv.25-26 and to the self-discipline ('I discipline my body') that wins it. Low volume; included as a coherent wisdom echo of the crown-as-reward-for-self-mastery.

echoes.text: For it was truly a divine contest which was carried through by them. For at that time virtue presided over the contest, approving the victory through endurance, namely, immortality, eternal life. Eleazar was the first to contend: and the mother of the seven children entered the contest; and the kindred contended. The tyrant was the opposite; and the world and living men were the spectators. And reverence for God conquered, and crowned her own athletes.
echoes.note: The martyr-contest imagery ('truly divine was the contest... virtue was the umpire, the prize was incorruptibility in long-lasting life... the world and humanity were the spectators') is a striking Second-Temple parallel to Paul's stadium, self-control, prize, and incorruptible crown (vv.24-27). Cited as availability evidence for the athletic-contest-for-incorruption topos; low volume, contested as a possibly later or independent development.

pericopes.text: Now I would not have you ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; and were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food; and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. However with most of them, God was not well pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.

echoes.text: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night: the pillar of cloud by day, and the pillar of fire by night, didn’t depart from before the people.
echoes.note: The pillar of cloud leading Israel is the referent of 'our fathers were all under the cloud.' High volume and availability; Paul reads the wilderness narrative typologically, making the cloud a figure of the divine covering shared by all. Coherence with the baptismal reading of v.2 confirms the allusion.

echoes.text: The angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud moved from before them, and stood behind them. It came between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel; and there was the cloud and the darkness, yet gave it light by night: and the one didn’t come near the other all the night.
echoes.note: The angel-and-cloud standing between Egypt and Israel at the sea supplies the dual cloud/sea imagery Paul fuses in vv.1-2. Recurrence of the cloud motif and its narrative pairing with the sea-crossing make this a strong contributor to 'under the cloud.'

echoes.text: On the day that the tabernacle was raised up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, even the Tent of the Testimony: and at evening it was over the tabernacle as it were the appearance of fire, until morning. So it was continually. The cloud covered it, and the appearance of fire by night. Whenever the cloud was taken up from over the Tent, then after that the children of Israel traveled; and in the place where the cloud remained, there the children of Israel […]
echoes.note: The cloud covering the tabernacle and regulating Israel's movements reinforces the 'under the cloud' language as a sustained guiding-presence motif, not a single event. Lower volume than Exodus 13 but adds recurrence to the cloud tradition Paul draws on.

echoes.text: He spread a cloud for a covering, fire to give light in the night.
echoes.note: 'He spread a cloud for a covering' summarizes the Exodus cloud in a single liturgical line that may stand closer to Paul's compressed phrasing than the narrative itself. The psalm's recital of wilderness mercies (cloud, sea, manna, water from the rock) parallels Paul's own catalogue, suggesting a psalmic mediation of the tradition.

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all the night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.
echoes.note: 'All passed through the sea' directly invokes the Red Sea crossing on dry ground between walls of water. High volume and availability; Paul makes the crossing a type of baptism (v.2), the controlling figural reading of the pericope.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: The manna is the 'spiritual food' all ate. The chapter's wilderness frame and Paul's emphasis on 'the same' food for all point to the daily bread from heaven. He reads it figurally as sacramental nourishment prefiguring Christ.

echoes.text: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky. Man ate the bread of angels. He sent them food to the full.
echoes.note: 'He rained down manna... grain of heaven... bread of the mighty' interprets the manna as heavenly bread, close to Paul's 'spiritual food.' The psalm's theological reading of the wilderness gifts coheres with Paul's, making it a plausible mediating source alongside Exodus 16.

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: 'Man does not live by bread alone... but by every word' interprets the manna as more than physical sustenance, supporting Paul's 'spiritual' qualifier. Moderate volume; the Deuteronomic theology of manna as God-given instruction coheres with Paul's sacramental reading.

echoes.text: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink.” Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.
echoes.note: Water struck from the rock at Horeb is the 'spiritual drink.' High volume; combined with Numbers 20 it grounds 'the Rock was Christ.' Paul's figural identification of the rock with Christ depends on these water-from-rock episodes.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Take the rod, and assemble the congregation, you, and Aaron your brother, and speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water. You shall bring water to them out of the rock; so you shall give the congregation and their livestock drink.” Moses took the rod from before Yahweh, as he commanded him. Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall […]
echoes.note: The second water-from-rock event at Meribah supplies the geographic span (beginning and end of the wilderness) that fuels the haggadic 'rock that followed them.' Recurrence of two rock-events at opposite ends of the journey underlies the moving-rock tradition Paul presupposes.

echoes.text: He split rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink abundantly as out of the depths. He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers.
echoes.note: 'He split rocks... brought streams... waters run down like rivers' poeticizes the water-from-rock miracle and may inform 'drank of a spiritual rock.' The psalm's abundance language coheres with Paul's claim that all drank the same drink.

echoes.text: He opened the rock, and waters gushed out. They ran as a river in the dry places.
echoes.note: 'He opened the rock, and water gushed out; it flowed through the desert like a river' depicts water following Israel through the wilderness, the nearest scriptural seed of the 'rock that followed them.' Strong coherence with the moving-water tradition Paul assumes.

echoes.text: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.
echoes.note: 'The Rock, his work is perfect' establishes the Song of Moses' titular use of 'the Rock' (haTsur) for God, the theological backbone of 'the Rock was Christ.' Paul's identification trades on this divine-Rock title, not merely the water episodes.

echoes.text: But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked. You have grown fat. You have grown thick. You have become sleek. Then he abandoned God who made him, and rejected the Rock of his salvation.
echoes.note: 'Forsook God... scoffed at the Rock of his salvation' continues the Song's Rock-title for God amid the very apostasy Paul is warning against. Recurrence within the Song he draws on elsewhere in the chapter (vv.17,21) strengthens the link.

echoes.text: Of the Rock who became your father, you are unmindful, and have forgotten God who gave you birth.
echoes.note: 'You forgot the Rock that bore you' adds the begetting-Rock image to the divine-Rock cluster. Low volume on its own, but it belongs to the Song of Moses substratum that pervades 1 Cor 10's rock and demon language.

echoes.text: How could one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, and Yahweh had delivered them up? For their rock is not as our Rock, even our enemies themselves concede.
echoes.note: 'Their Rock had sold them... their rock is not as our Rock' juxtaposes Israel's God-Rock against the enemies' rock, sharpening the Rock title. Faint here but coheres with Paul's polemical use of Deut 32 across the chapter.

echoes.text: Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness; and all who were numbered of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have murmured against me, surely you shall not come into the land, concerning which I swore that I would make you dwell therein, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.
echoes.note: 'Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness' is the source of 'they were overthrown in the wilderness' (v.5). High volume and verbal coherence with kateströthēsan; the wilderness-generation's exclusion is Paul's typological warning to the Corinthians.

echoes.text: ‘Because Yahweh was not able to bring this people into the land which he swore to them, therefore he has slain them in the wilderness.’
echoes.note: 'The LORD was not able to bring this people in... he slaughtered them in the wilderness' supplies the 'God was not well pleased' / 'overthrown' theme. Coherence with v.5's divine displeasure motif.

echoes.text: when the anger of God went up against them, killed some of their fattest, and struck down the young men of Israel.
echoes.note: 'The anger of God came up against them... and struck down... the young men of Israel' poeticizes the wilderness destruction Paul invokes in v.5. The psalm's wilderness-judgment recital parallels Paul's whole catalogue.

echoes.text: Forty long years I was grieved with that generation, and said, “It is a people that errs in their heart. They have not known my ways.” Therefore I swore in my wrath, “They won’t enter into my rest.”
echoes.note: 'Forty years... they shall not enter my rest' expresses God's displeasure with the wilderness generation, matching 'God was not well pleased.' A liturgical summary of the very judgment Paul applies typologically.

pericopes.text: Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted. Neither be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Neither let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them committed, and in one day twenty-three thousand fell. Neither let us test the Lord, as some of them tested, and perished by the serpents. Neither grumble, as some of them also grumbled, and perished by the destroyer.

echoes.text: The mixed multitude that was among them lusted exceedingly: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, “Who will give us flesh to eat?
echoes.note: 'The rabble had a strong craving... who will give us meat to eat?' grounds 'we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted' (v.6). The verb epethymēsan echoes the craving narrative; coherence with the wilderness-craving judgment.

echoes.text: The name of that place was called Kibroth Hattaavah, because there they buried the people who lusted.
echoes.note: Kibroth-hattaavah, 'the graves of craving,' names the place where the people who lusted were buried, the etiological seed of Paul's 'lust after evil things.' High coherence with v.6's craving-and-death pattern.

echoes.text: but gave in to craving in the desert, and tested God in the wasteland.
echoes.note: 'They lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tested God in the desert' compactly pairs lust and testing, both of which Paul enumerates (vv.6,9). The psalm's wilderness-sin catalogue is a likely template for Paul's list.

echoes.text: They rose up early on the next day, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.
echoes.note: 'The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play' is quoted verbatim (v.7) from the golden-calf episode, marked 'as it is written.' Highest volume; the calf is Paul's paradigm of idolatry feasting, directly relevant to the idol-meat question.

echoes.text: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron, and said to him, “Come, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.” Aaron said to them, “Take off the golden rings, which are in the ears of your wives, of your sons, and of your daughters, and bring them to me.” All the people […]
echoes.note: The golden-calf narrative as a whole supplies 'neither be idolaters, as some of them were' (v.7). The calf is the controlling type of idolatrous communal feasting that frames Paul's argument about meals offered to idols.

echoes.text: Israel stayed in Shittim; and the people began to play the prostitute with the daughters of Moab; for they called the people to the sacrifices of their gods. The people ate and bowed down to their gods. Israel joined himself to Baal Peor. Yahweh’s anger was kindled against Israel. Yahweh said to Moses, “Take all the chiefs of the people, and hang them up to Yahweh before the sun, that the fierce anger of Yahweh may turn away from Israel.” Moses said to […]
echoes.note: The Baal-Peor apostasy, where Israel committed sexual immorality with Moabite women and a plague killed many, is the type behind v.8. High volume and coherence; Paul's 23,000 reworks the Numbers death toll for his warning against porneia.

echoes.text: Those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.
echoes.note: Numbers reports 24,000 dead 'in one day'; Paul's 'twenty-three thousand fell in one day' alludes to this figure, the difference being a known harmonization crux. The 'in one day' phrase strengthens the verbal tie even as the number varies.

echoes.text: The people spoke against God, and against Moses, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no bread, and there is no water; and our soul loathes this light bread.” Yahweh sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people. Many people of Israel died.
echoes.note: The fiery serpents sent because the people spoke against God supply 'perished by the serpents' (v.9). High volume; the serpent plague is the type for testing God/Christ, directly named by Paul.

echoes.text: They tempted God in their heart by asking food according to their desire.
echoes.note: 'They tested God in their heart by asking food' offers the 'test' vocabulary Paul uses in v.9. Faint, but coheres with the psalmic wilderness-testing tradition behind his catalogue.

echoes.text: But on the next day all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, “You have killed Yahweh’s people!” When the congregation was assembled against Moses and against Aaron, They looked toward the Tent of Meeting. Behold, the cloud covered it, and Yahweh’s glory appeared. Moses and Aaron came to the front of the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Get away from among this congregation, that I may […]
echoes.note: After Korah, the congregation grumbled against Moses and Aaron and a plague (stopped by the destroyer/atonement) killed 14,700, the type behind 'neither grumble... perished by the destroyer' (v.10). High coherence between the grumbling-then-plague pattern and Paul's clause.

echoes.text: All the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt, or that we had died in this wilderness!
echoes.note: 'All the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron' supplies the murmuring motif that ends in wilderness death. Plausible alongside Num 16 as the referent for 'as some of them also grumbled.'

echoes.text: For Yahweh will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood on the lintel, and on the two door posts, Yahweh will pass over the door, and will not allow the destroyer to come in to your houses to strike you.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will not allow the destroyer to enter' names ha-mashchit, 'the destroyer,' the agent Paul invokes in v.10. The Passover destroyer is reapplied to the wilderness-grumbling judgment, supplying Paul's exact figure.

pericopes.text: Now all these things happened to them by way of example, and they were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come. Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall. No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

echoes.text: even those men who brought up an evil report of the land, died by the plague before Yahweh.
echoes.note: The death of the faithless spies 'by a plague before the LORD' caps the wilderness judgments Paul says 'happened to them by way of example' (v.11). Faint summary tie reinforcing the typological frame, not a specific verbal echo.

echoes.text: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not.
echoes.note: 'Remember the whole way the LORD led you... to test you' frames the wilderness as instructive testing, coherent with 'written for our admonition' and the temptation theme of v.13. Low volume; offered for the didactic-wilderness coherence.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: 'Know that the LORD your God is the faithful God' underlies 'God is faithful' (v.13). The covenant-faithfulness predicate is a Deuteronomic commonplace Paul likely draws on for assurance amid testing.

pericopes.text: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to wise men. Judge what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless, isn’t it a sharing of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, isn’t it a sharing of the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread. Consider Israel according to the flesh. Don’t those who eat the sacrifices participate in the altar? What am I saying then? That a thing sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? But I say that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God, and I don’t desire that you would have fellowship with demons. You can’t both drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You can’t both partake of the table of the Lord, and of the table of demons. Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

echoes.text: The flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning.
echoes.note: The peace/fellowship offering whose flesh the offerer eats grounds 'those who eat the sacrifices participate in the altar' (v.18). The shared-meal logic of the well-being offering is Paul's analogy for koinonia at the altar.

echoes.text: Every male among the priests may eat of it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy.
echoes.note: 'Every male among the priests may eat of it... it is most holy' establishes that eating the sacrifice joins one to the altar's holiness, the premise of v.18. Coherence with Paul's participation argument.

echoes.text: You shall eat before Yahweh your God, in the place which he chooses, to cause his name to dwell there, the tithe of your grain, of your new wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock; that you may learn to fear Yahweh your God always. If the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry it, because the place is too far from you, which Yahweh your God shall choose, to set his name there, when Yahweh your God shall […]
echoes.note: Eating the tithe and sacrifices 'before the LORD' as a covenant meal supports Paul's table-of-the-Lord/participation theme (vv.18,21). Faint; offered for the sacrificial-meal coherence rather than verbal contact.

echoes.text: They sacrificed to demons, not God, to gods that they didn’t know, to new gods that came up recently, which your fathers didn’t dread.
echoes.note: 'They sacrificed to demons, not God' (Song of Moses) is the source of 'the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God' (v.20), near-verbatim. High volume; the Song's demon-sacrifice charge is the scriptural warrant for Paul's whole idol-meat verdict.

echoes.text: Yes, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.
echoes.note: 'They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons' parallels Deut 32:17 and reinforces 'sacrifice to demons' (v.20). The psalm's wilderness-and-conquest demon-sacrifice motif coheres with Paul's reading; a likely secondary source.

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: 'They have made me jealous with what is no god' is the direct backdrop to 'do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?' (v.22). Recurrence within the Song of Moses (with v.17) and verbal contact on jealousy/provocation make this a strong, deliberate echo.

echoes.text: for you shall worship no other god: for Yahweh, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.
echoes.note: 'The LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God' grounds the jealousy logic of v.22 and ties the idolatry warning to the covenant's first commandment. Coheres with the jealous-God theology Paul presses against idol feasts.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'There is no god beside me' / unmatched divine power may color 'Are we stronger than he?' (v.22). Faint, but consistent with Paul's sustained use of the Song of Moses in this section.

echoes.text: You offer polluted bread on my altar. You say, ‘How have we polluted you?’ In that you say, ‘Yahweh’s table is contemptible.’
echoes.note: 'The table of the LORD' as the altar offers the only OT 'table of the Lord' phrase behind v.21's 'table of the Lord.' Low volume and uncertain, but the unique idiom warrants noting.

pericopes.text: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are profitable. “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good. Whatever is sold in the butcher shop, eat, asking no question for the sake of conscience, for “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” But if one of those who don’t believe invites you to a meal, and you are inclined to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. But if anyone says to you, “This was offered to idols,” don’t eat it for the sake of the one who told you, and for the sake of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and all its fullness.” Conscience, I say, not your own, but the other’s conscience. For why is my liberty judged by another conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced for that for which I give thanks?

echoes.text: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.
echoes.note: 'The earth is the LORD's, and its fullness' is quoted verbatim (v.26) and repeated at v.28 as the warrant that all food is clean for the believer. Highest volume; the creation-belongs-to-God claim is Paul's decisive ground for eating market meat.

echoes.text: If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine, and all that is in it.
echoes.note: 'The world is mine, and its fullness' restates the same creation-ownership claim as Ps 24:1 and could stand behind v.26's wording. Lower probability given the near-exact match to Ps 24:1, but noted for the shared 'fullness' idiom.

pericopes.text: Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Give no occasions for stumbling, either to Jews, or to Greeks, or to the assembly of God; even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.

echoes.text: everyone who is called by my name, and whom I have created for my glory, whom I have formed, yes, whom I have made.’”
echoes.note: 'Everyone... whom I created for my glory' may inform 'do all to the glory of God' (v.31). Faint and thematic; offered for the creation-for-God's-glory coherence behind Paul's doxological maxim.

pericopes.text: Now I praise you, brothers, that you remember me in all things, and hold firm the traditions, even as I delivered them to you. But I would have you know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God. Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonors his head. But every woman praying or prophesying with her head unveiled dishonors her head. For it is one and the same thing as if she were shaved. For if a woman is not covered, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be covered. For a man indeed ought not to have his head covered, because he is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man; for neither was man created for the woman, but woman for the man. For this cause the woman ought to have authority on her head, because of the angels. Nevertheless, neither is the woman independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman, in the Lord. For as woman came from man, so a man also comes through a woman; but all things are from God. Judge for yourselves. Is it appropriate that a woman pray to God unveiled? Doesn’t even nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a dishonor to him? But if a woman has long hair, it is a glory to her, for her hair is given to her for a covering. But if any man seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither do God’s assemblies.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: Paul's claim that man 'is the image and glory of God' (v.7) draws directly on the creation of humanity in God's image and likeness. The Greek eikon echoes LXX Gen 1:26-27. High volume and coherence; Paul reasons from the creation account to gender relations in worship.

echoes.text: Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.” Out of the ground Yahweh God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name. The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper […]
echoes.note: Verses 8-9 ('man is not from woman, but woman from man... neither was man created for the woman, but woman for the man') paraphrase the formation of woman from Adam's rib and as a helper fit for him. Explicit appeal to the order of creation; very high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The framing of man as formed first and woman 'from man' (v.8) presupposes the prior molding of Adam from the dust in Gen 2:7, the immediate context of the woman's formation. Faint and dependent on the larger Gen 2 narrative already in view.

echoes.text: When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.” The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children […]
echoes.note: The enigmatic 'because of the angels' (v.10) has long been read against the sons of God who took human women, implying that uncovered women in worship could provoke angelic lust. A major interpretive option but contested; volume is low since Paul gives no quotation, only the cryptic phrase.

echoes.text: I will give you thanks with my whole heart. Before the gods, I will sing praises to you.
echoes.note: An alternative reading of 'because of the angels' (v.10) is that angels are present at communal worship (cf. praising God 'before the gods/angels'), so propriety must be maintained in their sight. Faint, contested, and one of several competing explanations.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: Second-Temple Watcher tradition (1 Enoch 6-7) elaborates Gen 6's angelic descent and lust for women, the most likely backdrop if 'the angels' (v.10) refers to fallen watchers. Availability is secure; recurrence in early Christian reception (Tertullian) supports it, but it remains contested.

pericopes.text: But in giving you this command, I don’t praise you, that you come together not for the better but for the worse. For first of all, when you come together in the assembly, I hear that divisions exist among you, and I partly believe it. For there also must be factions among you, that those who are approved may be revealed among you. When therefore you assemble yourselves together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken. What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly, and put them to shame who don’t have? What shall I tell you? Shall I praise you? In this I don’t praise you.

echoes.text: You shall rejoice before Yahweh your God: you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, the Levite who is within your gates, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are in your midst, in the place which Yahweh your God shall choose to cause his name to dwell there. You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt. You shall observe and do these statutes. You shall keep the feast of tents seven days, after you have […]
echoes.note: Paul's rebuke that the rich shame 'those who have nothing' at the common meal (v.22) coheres with the Torah's repeated insistence that festal eating include the poor, the stranger, the widow. Faint thematic echo rather than a specific citation; no verbal overlap.

echoes.text: Woe to those who rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; who stay late into the night, until wine inflames them! The harp, lyre, tambourine, and flute, with wine, are at their feasts; but they don’t respect the work of Yahweh, neither have they considered the operation of his hands.
echoes.note: The picture of some drunken while others go hungry at the assembly (vv.21-22) recalls prophetic woes against feasting and drunkenness that ignore covenant obligation. Low volume; a moral-prophetic resonance, not a quotation.

pericopes.text: For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread. When he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.” In the same way he also took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.” For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' (v.25) fuses Moses' words at Sinai, 'the blood of the covenant,' with covenant-inauguration sacrifice. High volume via the covenant+blood pairing and strong coherence; the Supper is presented as a covenant-ratifying meal.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
echoes.note: The phrase 'the new covenant' (v.25) is verbatim from Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant (LXX Jer 38:31). Highest volume of any echo here; Jesus' cup-word interprets the Supper as the inauguration of Jeremiah's promised covenant.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: The institution 'on the night in which he was betrayed' (v.23) over bread and cup is set within the Passover frame; the memorial meal ('in memory of me') echoes the Passover's perpetual remembrance. Coherence is strong, though the verbal overlap is thematic rather than quoted.

echoes.text: This day shall be to you for a memorial, and you shall keep it a feast to Yahweh: throughout your generations you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever.
echoes.note: 'Do this in memory of me' (vv.24-25) mirrors the Passover ordinance that the day be a 'memorial' (zikkaron / LXX mnemosynon) kept perpetually. The memorial-meal logic transfers from Exodus to the Lord's Supper.

echoes.text: As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the pit in which is no water.
echoes.note: 'By the blood of your covenant I have set your prisoners free' is one possible background for 'the new covenant in my blood' (v.25), linking covenant blood to liberation. Faint and secondary to Exodus 24/Jeremiah 31; low volume.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The body 'which is for you' and proclaiming the Lord's death (vv.24, 26) may echo the Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and bore others' sin. Low volume, contested; resonance is conceptual rather than verbal in this passage.

pericopes.text: Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way unworthy of the Lord will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread, and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment to himself, if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body. For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep. For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn’t be judged. But when we are judged, we are punished by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world. Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. But if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, lest your coming together be for judgment. The rest I will set in order whenever I come.

echoes.text: Examine me, Yahweh, and prove me. Try my heart and my mind.
echoes.note: 'Let a man examine himself' (v.28) echoes the psalmist's plea, 'Examine me, O Lord, and prove me; test my heart and my mind.' Self-scrutiny before approaching God is the shared logic; medium volume given the verbal field of testing/proving.

echoes.text: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
echoes.note: The call to self-examination before the cup (v.28) coheres with 'Search me, O God, and know my heart... see if there is any wicked way in me.' Recurrence of the examine-the-heart motif in the Psalter supports the echo.

echoes.text: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the Lord' parallels Paul's 'if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn't be judged' (v.31). The self-examination-averts-judgment logic is closely coherent with Lamentations' penitential exhortation.

echoes.text: You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.
echoes.note: 'When we are judged, we are punished by the Lord' (v.32) draws on the covenant principle that the Lord disciplines his people 'as a man disciplines his son.' The corrective (not condemnatory) character of the chastening matches Paul's point.

echoes.text: My son, don’t despise Yahweh’s discipline, neither be weary of his reproof: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
echoes.note: Being 'punished by the Lord' so as not to be condemned (v.32) echoes 'do not despise the Lord's discipline... for the Lord reproves him whom he loves.' Strong coherence with the fatherly-discipline theme; medium volume.
echoes.lxxText: My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loves, he rebukes, and scourges every son whom he receives.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs. Don’t eat it raw, nor boiled at all with water, but roasted with fire; with its head, its legs and its inner parts. You shall let nothing of it remain until the morning; but that which remains of it until the morning you shall burn with fire. This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your […]
echoes.note: The instruction to 'wait for one another' and eat at home if hungry (vv.33-34) may faintly echo the ordered, communal eating of the Passover within households. Low volume and contested; primarily a practical instruction.

echoes.text: For when they were tried, albeit but in mercy chastened, They learned how the ungodly were tormented, being judged with wrath: For these, as a father, admonishing them, you did prove; But those, as a stern king, condemning them, you did search out.
echoes.note: The idea that God's people are tested/disciplined as a father admonishes while the wicked are condemned (vv.31-32) parallels Wisdom's contrast of the Lord chastening Israel in mercy versus judging the ungodly in wrath. Deuterocanonical resonance; low volume, contested.

pericopes.text: Now concerning spiritual things, brothers, I don’t want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were heathen, you were led away to those mute idols, however you might be led. Therefore I make known to you that no man speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus is accursed.” No one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” but by the Holy Spirit.

echoes.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat.
echoes.note: Paul recalls the Corinthians being led to 'mute idols' (eidola aphona), echoing the psalm's taunt that the nations' idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands, with mouths that cannot speak. The motif of the idol's speechlessness contrasted with the living God is a fixed OT polemic, and the verbal link (mouths/speech) gives this strong volume.

echoes.text: “What value does the engraved image have, that its maker has engraved it; the molten image, even the teacher of lies, that he who fashions its form trusts in it, to make mute idols? Woe to him who says to the wood, ‘Awake!’ or to the mute stone, ‘Arise!’ Shall this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in its midst.
echoes.note: The dumb idol that cannot teach, the woe to one who says to a mute stone 'Awake,' undergirds Paul's phrase 'mute idols.' Habakkuk stresses that there is no breath/spirit in the idol, which sharpens Paul's contrast with the speaking, Spirit-empowered confession 'Jesus is Lord' that follows.

echoes.text: They bear it on the shoulder, they carry it, and set it in its place, and it stands, from its place it shall not move: yes, one may cry to it, yet it can not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.
echoes.note: Isaiah mocks the idol that is carried, set in place, and cannot move or answer when cried to; it does not save. Paul's image of being 'led away to mute idols, however you might be led' coheres with this picture of a powerless, voiceless god, reinforcing the speech/no-speech antithesis.

echoes.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they can’t speak. They have eyes, but they can’t see. They have ears, but they can’t hear; neither is there any breath in their mouths.
echoes.note: A close parallel to Psalm 115, again ridiculing idols with mouths that do not speak and no breath in their mouths. Its recurrence in the same idol-polemic tradition raises the volume of the 'mute idols' echo, though the verbal contact is generic.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: Paul's claim that only by the Holy Spirit can one confess 'Jesus is Lord' anticipates the chapter's pneumatology, faintly resting on the promise that God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh so that they prophesy. The connection is thematic (Spirit-enabled speech) rather than verbal here.

pericopes.text: Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord. There are various kinds of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: The 'varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit' poured out on the community reflects the eschatological outpouring of one Spirit producing diverse manifestations (sons, daughters, old, young prophesying and dreaming). The one-Spirit/many-recipients structure coheres tightly with Joel's vision, which Paul elsewhere cites for the Spirit's universal distribution.

echoes.text: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]
echoes.note: God takes of the one Spirit on Moses and distributes it among the seventy elders, who then prophesy; Moses wishes all the Lord's people were prophets. This is the paradigmatic OT scene of one Spirit apportioned to many for varied ministry, mapping onto Paul's 'same Spirit... various kinds of service.'

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The Spirit of the Lord resting as a sevenfold endowment (wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, fear) on the messianic shoot offers a precedent for one Spirit yielding plural gifts. The catalog form is suggestive, though Paul's list differs in content.

pericopes.text: But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, and to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another faith, by the same Spirit; and to another gifts of healings, by the same Spirit; and to another workings of miracles; and to another prophecy; and to another discerning of spirits; to another different kinds of languages; and to another the interpretation of languages. But the one and the same Spirit works all of these, distributing to each one separately as he desires.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: Paul's enumeration of Spirit-gifts beginning with 'word of wisdom' and 'word of knowledge' echoes the messianic Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, and knowledge. Both passages catalog distinct charisms flowing from a single divine Spirit, giving coherence to the allusion even where the lists do not match item-for-item.

echoes.text: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]
echoes.note: The Spirit distributed by God among many recipients, each prophesying, anticipates Paul's 'distributing to each one separately as he desires.' The sovereign apportioning of one Spirit to diverse people for prophecy and service is the structural backbone shared with the Mosaic narrative.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: Prophecy as the signature gift of the poured-out Spirit ('your sons and daughters shall prophesy') stands behind Paul's list, which prominently includes prophecy. The eschatological democratization of the Spirit coheres with Paul's 'to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit.'

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we desired of you; for you have made known to us the king’s matter.
echoes.note: Daniel praises God who gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding, and reveals deep and hidden things. The pairing of God-given 'wisdom' and 'knowledge' as revelatory gifts faintly parallels Paul's first two charisms, though no verbal citation is made.

echoes.text: and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
echoes.note: God fills Bezalel with the Spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all craftsmanship for the tabernacle. This is the OT prototype of the Spirit equipping individuals with specific skill-gifts for the building of God's dwelling, resonating with Paul's Spirit-distributed abilities for the body's upbuilding.

echoes.text: For she that is the architect of all things taught me, even wisdom. For there is in her a spirit quick of understanding, holy, Alone in kind, manifold, Subtil, freely moving, Clear in utterance, unpolluted, Distinct, unharmed, Loving what is good, keen, unhindered, Beneficent, loving toward man, Stedfast, sure, free from care, All-powerful, all-surveying, And penetrating through all spirits That are quick of understanding, pure, most subtle:
echoes.note: Wisdom describes the spirit of wisdom as manifold (poikilos), intelligent, all-powerful, pervading all spirits, distributing benefits. The notion of one Spirit with manifold operations apportioned among many coheres with Paul's 'various kinds of gifts... the one and the same Spirit works all,' making a Second-Temple sapiential backdrop plausible.

pericopes.text: For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: Being 'all given to drink into one Spirit' and 'baptized in one Spirit' draws on the imagery of the Spirit poured out on all flesh regardless of status (sons, daughters, slaves). Joel's leveling of social distinctions in the Spirit's outpouring coheres with Paul's 'whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free.'

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: God promises to pour water on the thirsty and his Spirit upon the offspring, joining the images of drinking/water and Spirit-outpouring. Paul's distinctive phrase 'all given to drink into one Spirit' coheres strongly with this water-Spirit fusion in the prophetic promise of renewal.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: God puts his one Spirit within the reconstituted people so that a scattered, divided house becomes one living body. The creation of a unified people animated by God's Spirit faintly underlies Paul's 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.'

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The one body formed and animated by the breath/Spirit of God offers a creational template for Paul's one Spirit constituting one living body. The link is figural rather than verbal, but Paul's body-and-Spirit pairing resonates with the animating-breath motif.

pericopes.text: For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot would say, “Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body,” it is not therefore not part of the body. If the ear would say, “Because I’m not the eye, I’m not part of the body,” it’s not therefore not part of the body. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be? But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired. If they were all one member, where would the body be? But now they are many members, but one body.

echoes.text: For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well. My frame wasn’t hidden from you, when I was made in secret, woven together in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.
echoes.note: The psalmist marvels that God formed and knit together his members in the womb, framing the body as God's deliberate composition. Paul's repeated 'God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired' coheres with this picture of divinely intended bodily arrangement, though the genre and vocabulary differ.

echoes.text: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
echoes.note: God's purposeful arrangement of each member 'just as he desired,' with each part necessary, faintly echoes the creation account in which God orders distinct parts and pronounces the whole very good. The connection is thematic (divine sovereign design) rather than lexical.

pericopes.text: The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.” No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary. Those parts of the body which we think to be less honorable, on those we bestow more abundant honor; and our unpresentable parts have more abundant propriety; whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part, that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. Or when one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

echoes.text: I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well. My frame wasn’t hidden from you, when I was made in secret, woven together in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.
echoes.note: The wisdom of how the body's members are formed and held in mutual dependence echoes the psalm's wonder at the body's intricate making. Paul's claim that God 'composed the body together' so members care for one another coheres with the psalm's sense of a divinely integrated body.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The command to love one's neighbor as oneself, grounding Israel's mutual solidarity, faintly underlies Paul's vision that members 'have the same care for one another' and suffer and rejoice together. The body imagery dramatizes the covenant ethic of corporate mutual care.

pericopes.text: Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually. God has set some in the assembly: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracle workers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, and various kinds of languages. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all miracle workers? Do all have gifts of healings? Do all speak with various languages? Do all interpret? But earnestly desire the best gifts. Moreover, I show a most excellent way to you.

echoes.text: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]
echoes.note: God's appointment of designated, Spirit-endowed offices in the assembly ('first apostles, second prophets, third teachers') recalls Moses' divinely appointed seventy who share the Spirit for leadership. Both depict God ordering a structured ministry among his people through the one Spirit.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: Prophets ranked among God's appointed in the assembly continues the chapter's reliance on Joel's outpoured-Spirit prophecy. The placement of prophecy as a settled, God-given office among the people coheres with the eschatological community of prophets Joel envisions.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: God's sovereign appointing and ordering of those he commissions ('I appointed you a prophet to the nations') faintly resonates with Paul's 'God has set some in the assembly.' The divine setting/appointing of ministers links the two, though no verbal citation is present.

pericopes.text: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal.

echoes.text: Praise him with loud cymbals! Praise him with resounding cymbals!
echoes.note: The 'clanging cymbal' (kymbalon alalazon) draws on the temple cymbals of the psalm's call to praise God with 'loud clashing cymbals.' Paul ironically inverts liturgical worship: cymbals were sanctioned only as accompaniment to true praise, so love-less ecstatic speech is mere noise, the percussion without the worship. Verbal and conceptual links give this high volume.

echoes.text: David spoke to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brothers the singers, with instruments of music, stringed instruments and harps and cymbals, sounding aloud and lifting up the voice with joy.
echoes.note: David appoints Levites with instruments, including cymbals, to raise sounds of joy in temple worship. Paul's 'clanging cymbal' presupposes this fixed liturgical role of the cymbal in Israelite praise; without love the sound is emptied of its cultic meaning. Recurrence of the cymbal across the Chronicler strengthens availability.

echoes.text: So the singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were given cymbals of brass to sound aloud;
echoes.note: Heman, Asaph, and Ethan sound bronze cymbals; the noun chalkos/'bronze' resonates with Paul's 'sounding brass' (chalkos echon). The pairing of brass and cymbal in one verse-pair (sounding brass, clanging cymbal) mirrors the Chronicler's pairing of bronze cymbals in temple music, though the link is faint.

echoes.text: Thus all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of Yahweh with shouting, and with sound of the cornet, and with trumpets, and with cymbals, sounding aloud with stringed instruments and harps.
echoes.note: All Israel brings up the ark with the sound of cymbals amid shouting (the verb cognate to alalazo). Paul's alalazon ('clanging') echoes the loud cultic shout/cymbal-clash of Israel's processional worship, here drained of substance when love is absent.

echoes.text: For you have made him a little lower than God, and crowned him with glory and honor.
echoes.note: 'Tongues of angels' presupposes the OT picture of angels (here 'a little lower than the angels/elohim') as a class of glorious heavenly beings whose speech surpasses human. The motif of angelic language is developed in Second-Temple texts; the canonical seedbed is the angelic praise tradition.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: Job's daughters receive cords enabling them to speak 'the dialect of angels' in hymnic praise. This pseudepigraphon attests the precise Second-Temple notion of distinct 'tongues of angels' that Paul invokes, supplying availability for his otherwise unparalleled phrase. Cited as cultural background, not a quoted source.

pericopes.text: If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.

echoes.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
echoes.note: 'So as to remove mountains' echoes the oracle to Zerubbabel, 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain,' where the mountain of obstacle is leveled not by might but by God's Spirit. The mountain-as-impediment removed by divine power coheres with Paul's faith that 'removes mountains.' Volume is moderate; the saying also circulated in dominical tradition.

echoes.text: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. The uneven shall be made level, and the rough places a plain.
echoes.note: 'Every mountain and hill shall be made low' supplies the eschatological image of mountains brought down before the coming of God. Paul's hyperbole of faith leveling mountains coheres with this prophetic flattening of obstacles, though the link is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: The stone cut without hands shatters the image and becomes a great mountain; the chapter's idiom of mysteries (raza) revealed undergirds Paul's 'know all mysteries.' The mountain motif here is faint, but Daniel's apocalyptic disclosure of 'mysteries' is the strongest OT seedbed for Paul's mysteria language.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
echoes.note: 'Know all mysteries and all knowledge' draws on Daniel's 'God in heaven who reveals mysteries,' the Aramaic raze that becomes the technical term for apocalyptic secrets. Paul's pairing of mysteries with prophetic gift coheres with Daniel's revealer-of-secrets, the principal OT source for the mystery-vocabulary.

pericopes.text: If I dole out all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.

echoes.text: Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his appearance was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He spoke, and commanded that they should heat the furnace seven times more than it was usually heated. He commanded certain mighty men who were in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace. Then these men were bound in their pants, their tunics, and their mantles, and their other […]
echoes.note: 'Give my body to be burned' evokes Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego handing over their bodies to the fiery furnace rather than worship the image. The willing surrender of the body to flames as the supreme act of devotion supplies the model Paul deems worthless without love. Strong thematic coherence with martyr-by-fire piety.

echoes.text: Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said, Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel, and delivered his servants who trusted in him, and have changed the king’s word, and have yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God.
echoes.note: The king praises the three who 'yielded up their bodies' rather than serve any god but their own; the LXX phrasing of surrendering the body parallels Paul's paradoso to soma mou. This sharpens the furnace allusion: bodily self-surrender is praiseworthy, yet Paul says even this profits nothing without love.

echoes.text: And when he was utterly maimed, the king commanded to bring him to the fire, being yet alive, and to fry him in the pan. And as the vapor of the pan spread far, they and their mother also exhorted one another to die nobly, saying thus:
echoes.note: The seven brothers are tortured and burned in pans for refusing apostasy, the paradigmatic deuterocanonical martyrdom by fire. Paul's 'give my body to be burned' coheres with this celebrated martyr-narrative of bodily immolation, a readily available exemplum in his milieu. Volume moderate, recurrence high in martyr tradition.

echoes.text: so, Eleazar, the descendant of Aaron, wasted away by the fire, did not give up his reasoning.
echoes.note: Eleazar likened to one consumed by fire yet conquering through reason and piety; the pseudepigraphal celebration of burning martyrdom as the height of virtue reinforces the cultural availability of Paul's burnt-body topos. Cited as background to the burning-as-supreme-sacrifice motif.

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: 'Dole out all my goods to feed the poor' resonates with the OT praise of the one who shares bread with the poor and is blessed. Paul concedes the highest almsgiving, yet subordinates it to love; the link to the wisdom ideal of generosity to the poor is thematic and faint.

pericopes.text: Love is patient and is kind; love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil; doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: 'Love is patient' (makrothymei) and 'kind' renders the LXX self-description of the LORD as 'slow to anger (makrothymos) and abounding in steadfast love.' Paul transposes the covenant attributes of God's character onto agape, so that the hymn portrays love with the very predicates of the divine name. High volume, strong coherence: the Exodus formula is the foundational OT portrait of patient, faithful love.

echoes.text: Yahweh is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and of great loving kindness.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and great in steadfast love' restates the Exodus formula and grounds Paul's 'love is patient and kind.' Its liturgical recurrence (Pss 86:15; 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2) gives the patient-and-kind pairing strong availability and volume as a fixed description of covenant love.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: 'Love covers all offenses' (versus hatred that stirs strife) underwrites Paul's 'love takes no account of evil' and 'bears all things.' The proverb's antithesis of love that overlooks wrongs against hate that provokes maps directly onto Paul's list of what love is not (provoked, resentful). The covering/non-reckoning of evil is a strong conceptual parallel.

echoes.text: and let none of you devise evil in your hearts against his neighbor, and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Do not devise evil in your hearts against one another... for all these things I hate' coheres with 'love takes no account of evil' and 'does not rejoice in unrighteousness.' Zechariah pairs the rejection of inward malice with truth-telling (8:16), matching Paul's contrast of evil-plotting against rejoicing in the truth.

echoes.text: He who covers an offense promotes love; but he who repeats a matter separates best friends.
echoes.note: 'Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates friends' parallels love that 'takes no account of evil' and 'bears all things.' The wisdom ideal of not rehearsing wrongs is a close conceptual match for Paul's non-reckoning love, reinforcing the Prov 10:12 covering-motif.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit.
echoes.note: 'Blessed is the one to whom the LORD imputes no iniquity' supplies the accounting idiom behind 'love takes no account of evil' (ou logizetai to kakon). Just as God's blessing rests on not-reckoning sin, Paul's love refuses to keep a ledger of wrongs; the logizomai/non-imputation link gives moderate verbal warrant.

echoes.text: He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who is hasty of spirit exalts folly' coheres with love that 'is not provoked' (ou paroxynetai). The wisdom valorization of slow anger against quick temper supports Paul's portrait, though without specific verbal contact.

echoes.text: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
echoes.note: 'Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall' undergirds love that 'doesn't brag, is not proud' (ou physioutai). The wisdom condemnation of arrogance is the broad OT seedbed for Paul's anti-boasting predicates, a thematic rather than verbal echo.

echoes.text: For she that is the architect of all things taught me, even wisdom. For there is in her a spirit quick of understanding, holy, Alone in kind, manifold, Subtil, freely moving, Clear in utterance, unpolluted, Distinct, unharmed, Loving what is good, keen, unhindered, Beneficent, loving toward man, Stedfast, sure, free from care, All-powerful, all-surveying, And penetrating through all spirits That are quick of understanding, pure, most subtle: For wisdom is […]
echoes.note: The hymn to Wisdom enumerates her attributes (kindly, loving the good, beneficent, unhindered) in a rhetorical catalogue strikingly like Paul's catalogue of love's attributes. As a Second-Temple model of personified virtue praised by predicate-lists, it offers availability for the form and ethos of Paul's encomium to agape.

echoes.text: Be not angry with your neighbor for every wrong; And do nothing by works of violence. Pride is hateful before the Lord and before men; And in the judgement of both will unrighteousness err. Sovereignty is transferred from nation to nation, Because of iniquities, and deeds of violence, and greed of money.
echoes.note: Ben Sira warns against bearing a grudge, against arrogance, and against the insolence (hyperephania) that God hates. The cluster of grudge-bearing, pride, and rude insolence parallels Paul's love that is 'not proud,' 'doesn't behave inappropriately,' and 'resentful,' giving deuterocanonical wisdom support for the vice-list love negates.

pericopes.text: doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;

echoes.text: Don’t rejoice when your enemy falls. Don’t let your heart be glad when he is overthrown;
echoes.note: 'Do not rejoice when your enemy falls' parallels love that 'doesn't rejoice in unrighteousness.' The wisdom prohibition of malicious joy at another's wrong/downfall is a close conceptual match for Paul's chairei... ou epi te adikia, supporting the contrast with rejoicing in the truth.

echoes.text: Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.
echoes.note: 'You delight in truth in the inward being' resonates with love that 'rejoices with the truth' (synchairei te aletheia). The OT pairing of God's delight in truth over against iniquity supports Paul's antithesis of unrighteousness and truth, though the verbal contact is loose.

pericopes.text: bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: 'Bears all things' (panta stegei) reprises the love-covers-all-offenses motif: stego ('cover/bear in silence') overlaps with the proverb's love that covers transgressions. The recurrence of the covering-language across 13:5 and 13:7 strengthens the link to the Proverbs source for love's forbearance.

echoes.text: It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD' coheres with love that 'hopes all things, endures all things' (panta hypomenei). The OT ideal of patient, hopeful endurance under affliction supplies the disposition Paul ascribes to love, a thematic echo of waiting-hope.

echoes.text: Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage' parallels love that 'hopes all things, endures all things.' The recurring OT summons to hopeful endurance and waiting on God undergirds Paul's panta elpizei, panta hypomenei as the posture of covenant trust.

pericopes.text: Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things. For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: 'Then face to face' draws on the LORD speaking with Moses 'mouth to mouth, clearly and not in dark speech (di' ainigmaton)'; Paul's 'in a mirror, dimly (en ainigmati)' uses the very LXX word from Numbers. The contrast of riddling/indirect sight now versus direct, unmediated vision then is grounded precisely in the Mosaic prerogative. High volume by the shared ainigma term.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. He turned again into the camp, but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.
echoes.note: 'The LORD used to speak to Moses face to face (prosopon kata prosopon), as one speaks to a friend' supplies Paul's exact phrase 'face to face' for the eschatological vision. The Mosaic privilege of direct divine encounter becomes the eschatological norm Paul anticipates, a strong verbal and conceptual link.

echoes.text: Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,
echoes.note: 'No prophet has arisen since like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face' reinforces the face-to-face idiom as the unique mode of unmediated knowledge of God. Paul universalizes this Mosaic singularity to all believers 'then,' so the prophetic incompleteness of 13:9 yields to Mosaic immediacy.

echoes.text: Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for, he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”
echoes.note: Jacob names Peniel, 'for I have seen God face to face (eidon... prosopon pros prosopon), and yet my life is preserved.'
