The patriarchal precedent of surviving a face-to-face vision of God feeds the OT 'face to face' tradition Paul invokes for final beatific sight. Recurrence of the idiom across Genesis-Deuteronomy strengthens availability.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether. You hem me in behind and before. You laid your hand on me. This knowledge is beyond me. It’s lofty. I can’t attain it.
echoes.note: 'Then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known' echoes the psalmist's confession that the LORD has searched and known him completely, his sitting and rising, his thoughts and ways, a knowledge 'too wonderful' to attain. Paul's epignosomai kathos kai epegnosthen inverts the asymmetry: now God knows me fully; then I will know likewise. Strong coherence with the OT theme of being exhaustively known by God.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you' contributes to the OT motif of God's prior, exhaustive knowledge of the person that underlies 'even as I was fully known' (epegnosthen). The divine foreknowing of the individual coheres with Paul's claim to be already fully known by God, a faint supporting echo.

echoes.text: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom is 'a spotless mirror (esoptron) of the working of God.' Paul's 'we see in a mirror' (di' esoptrou) shares the rare mirror-as-medium-of-divine-knowledge image; the deuterocanonical sapiential mirror supplies availability for Paul's epistemological metaphor of indirect present sight.

echoes.text: “But where shall wisdom be found? Where is the place of understanding? Man doesn’t know its price; Neither is it found in the land of the living. The deep says, ‘It isn’t in me.’ The sea says, ‘It isn’t with me.’ It can’t be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for its price. It can’t be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire. Gold and glass can’t equal it, neither shall it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold. […]
echoes.note: 'Where shall wisdom be found?'—it is hidden, known fully only to God who sees the ends of the earth. The wisdom poem's contrast of human partial knowledge against God's complete knowing coheres with Paul's 'we know in part' giving way to full knowledge, a thematic echo of the limits of present human cognition.

pericopes.text: But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'The righteous shall live by his faith(fulness)' supplies the OT root of Paul's enduring 'faith' (pistis) in the triad faith-hope-love that 'remains.' The prophetic grounding of life in abiding faith coheres with Paul's claim that faith abides into the eschaton, a thematic rather than verbal echo.

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: 'To do justice, and to love kindness (chesed), and to walk humbly with your God' offers an OT triad of enduring religious requirements culminating in covenant love. The form of a compressed triad whose summit is love/chesed loosely anticipates Paul's faith-hope-love crowned by the greatest, love. Faint formal echo.

pericopes.text: Follow after love, and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. For he who speaks in another language speaks not to men, but to God; for no one understands; but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries. But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation. He who speaks in another language edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the assembly. Now I desire to have you all speak with other languages, but rather that you would prophesy. For he is greater who prophesies than he who speaks with other languages, unless he interprets, that the assembly may be built up.

echoes.text: Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all Yahweh’s people were prophets, that Yahweh would put his Spirit on them!”
echoes.note: Paul's wish that 'you all' would prophesy (14:5) echoes Moses' cry, 'Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!' Both texts democratize prophecy against a restrictive view, and both tie prophecy to the bestowal of the Spirit. The coherence with Joel's poured-out-Spirit hope strengthens the link, though Paul does not cite Moses verbatim.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: The whole chapter's premise that ordinary believers prophesy when the Spirit comes draws on Joel's promise that sons, daughters, and servants will prophesy in the last days. Availability is secure (a foundational restoration text) and the theme recurs across Acts 2 and Paul; the echo is thematic rather than verbal here.

pericopes.text: But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking with other languages, what would I profit you, unless I speak to you either by way of revelation, or of knowledge, or of prophesying, or of teaching? Even things without life, giving a voice, whether pipe or harp, if they didn’t give a distinction in the sounds, how would it be known what is piped or harped? For if the trumpet gave an uncertain sound, who would prepare himself for war? So also you, unless you uttered by the tongue words easy to understand, how would it be known what is spoken? For you would be speaking into the air. There are, it may be, so many kinds of sounds in the world, and none of them is without meaning. If then I don’t know the meaning of the sound, I would be to him who speaks a foreigner, and he who speaks would be a foreigner to me. So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek that you may abound to the building up of the assembly.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Make two trumpets of silver. You shall make them of beaten work. You shall use them for the calling of the congregation, and for the journeying of the camps. When they blow them, all the congregation shall gather themselves to you at the door of the Tent of Meeting. If they blow just one, then the princes, the heads of the thousands of Israel, shall gather themselves to you. When you blow an alarm, the camps that lie on the […]
echoes.note: The trumpet that gives 'an uncertain sound' so that no one prepares for war (14:8) draws on the silver trumpets of Numbers 10, whose distinct blasts signal assembly, march, and battle. The whole rationale of Paul's analogy—that a sound must be intelligible to function—depends on the OT institution where a clear trumpet-call summons Israel to war and worship. Volume and coherence are strong.

echoes.text: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand:
echoes.note: The trumpet 'for war' and alarm imagery (14:8) coheres with Joel's command to 'Blow the trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm,' the paradigmatic intelligible warning-blast. The link reinforces the Numbers trumpet motif but is secondary; Paul's point about distinct sounds matches the prophetic alarm-trumpet's purpose of rousing the people.

echoes.text: Praise him with the sounding of the trumpet! Praise him with harp and lyre! Praise him with tambourine and dancing! Praise him with stringed instruments and flute! Praise him with loud cymbals! Praise him with resounding cymbals!
echoes.note: The lifeless instruments giving voice—pipe and harp (14:7)—recall the catalog of worship instruments in Psalm 150, where trumpet, harp, and pipe sound praise. The connection is faint and topical (musical instruments) rather than argumentative, and Paul's point is the opposite (sound without distinction is useless), so this is a contested, low-volume echo.

pericopes.text: Therefore let him who speaks in another language pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in another language, my spirit prays, but my understanding is unfruitful. What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also. I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also. Otherwise if you bless with the spirit, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say the “Amen” at your giving of thanks, seeing he doesn’t know what you say? For you most certainly give thanks well, but the other person is not built up. I thank my God, I speak with other languages more than you all. However in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might instruct others also, than ten thousand words in another language.

echoes.text: For God is the King of all the earth. Sing praises with understanding.
echoes.note: Paul's resolve to 'sing with the spirit and sing with the understanding also' (14:15) faintly echoes the Psalmist's 'sing praises with understanding' (maskil), the OT ideal of intelligent, comprehending praise. Volume is low and the verbal overlap rests on the Greek of the LXX, but the coherence with Paul's whole emphasis on the mind in worship makes it plausible.

echoes.text: and Ezra blessed Yahweh, the great God. All the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” with the lifting up of their hands. They bowed their heads, and worshiped Yahweh with their faces to the ground.
echoes.note: The congregational 'Amen' at the giving of thanks (14:16) reflects the liturgical practice exemplified when Ezra blessed the LORD and 'all the people answered, Amen, Amen,' lifting their hands. The motif of the assembly's responsive Amen is an OT/Second-Temple liturgical convention Paul assumes; the echo is institutional rather than a citation.

echoes.text: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting. All the people said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh.
echoes.note: The corporate 'Amen' sealing thanksgiving (14:16) also parallels 'all the people said, Amen, and praised the LORD' at David's psalm of thanks. Together with Nehemiah 8 and the Psalter's doxological Amens this establishes the availability of the responsive-Amen practice; a faint, contested echo.

pericopes.text: Brothers, don’t be children in thoughts, yet in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature. In the law it is written, “By men of strange languages and by the lips of strangers I will speak to this people. Not even thus will they hear me, says the Lord.” Therefore other languages are for a sign, not to those who believe, but to the unbelieving; but prophesying is for a sign, not to the unbelieving, but to those who believe. If therefore the whole assembly is assembled together and all speak with other languages, and unlearned or unbelieving people come in, won’t they say that you are crazy? But if all prophesy, and someone unbelieving or unlearned comes in, he is reproved by all, and he is judged by all. And thus the secrets of his heart are revealed. So he will fall down on his face and worship God, declaring that God is among you indeed.

echoes.text: But he will speak to this nation with stammering lips and in another language; to whom he said, “This is the resting place. Give rest to weary”; and “This is the refreshing”; yet they would not hear.
echoes.note: Paul formally cites this as 'in the law it is written': 'By men of strange languages and by the lips of strangers I will speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord' (14:21). Isaiah threatens that God will address mocking Judah through the unintelligible speech of Assyrian conquerors—a judgment of incomprehension—which Paul applies to tongues as a sign for unbelievers. The volume is maximal and the citation explicit, though Paul's wording diverges from both MT and LXX.

echoes.text: You will no longer see the fierce people, a people of a deep speech that you can’t comprehend, with a strange language that you can’t understand.
echoes.note: The motif of a foreign people 'of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend, stammering in a tongue you cannot understand' undergirds Paul's theology of unintelligible foreign tongues as a sign of judgment (14:21-22). It coheres with the Isaiah 28 citation as part of the prophet's strange-tongues-as-judgment complex, supplying the conceptual frame even if Paul quotes 28:11-12 directly.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: “The labor of Egypt, and the merchandise of Ethiopia, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you, and they shall be yours. They will go after you. They shall come over in chains; and they will bow down to you. They will make supplication to you: ‘Surely God is in you; and there is no one else. There is no other god.
echoes.note: The outsider's confession that 'God is among you indeed' (14:25) echoes Isaiah's prophecy that the nations will bow down and confess of Israel, 'God is in you only, and there is no other God.' Both involve Gentiles falling down and acknowledging the true God's presence among his people; the eschatological-pilgrimage frame matches Paul's scene of conviction precisely.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “In those days, ten men will take hold, out of all the languages of the nations, they will take hold of the skirt of him who is a Jew, saying, ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.’”
echoes.note: The unbeliever convicted and declaring God's presence (14:25) draws on Zechariah's vision that ten men from the nations will grasp a Jew's garment, saying, 'We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' The shared element—an outsider's confession 'God is with/among you'—aligns with Paul's portrait of prophecy drawing in the unbeliever to worship.

echoes.text: The king answered to Daniel, and said, Of a truth your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, since you have been able to reveal this secret.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar's falling and confession to Daniel—'Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, a revealer of mysteries'—parallels the unbeliever falling on his face when 'the secrets of his heart are revealed' (14:25). Both pair the disclosure of hidden things with a pagan ruler's prostration and confession of the true God; the revelation-of-secrets motif strengthens the coherence.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: That prophecy lays bare 'the secrets of his heart' (14:25) reflects the conviction that the LORD looks not on outward appearance but 'on the heart.' The OT premise that God alone discerns the hidden heart underwrites Paul's claim that prophetic speech exposes inner secrets; a thematic echo rather than a citation.

echoes.text: won’t God search this out? For he knows the secrets of the heart.
echoes.note: 'God knows the secrets of the heart' supplies the same conviction behind 14:25—the disclosure of hidden things by divine knowledge. Volume is low and the link general, but it reinforces the OT availability of the searched-heart theme alongside 1 Samuel 16:7 and Psalm 139.

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: The unbeliever 'will fall down on his face and worship God' (14:25) coheres with Isaiah's oracle that 'to me every knee shall bow,' the prophetic vision of universal prostration before the LORD. Faint and contested, but part of the same Isaiah 45 confession-of-the-nations complex Paul is drawing on.

pericopes.text: What is it then, brothers? When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, has an interpretation. Let all things be done to build each other up. If any man speaks in another language, let it be two, or at the most three, and in turn; and let one interpret. But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the assembly, and let him speak to himself, and to God. Let the prophets speak, two or three, and let the others discern. But if a revelation is made to another sitting by, let the first keep silent. For you all can prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be exhorted. The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets, for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace. As in all the assemblies of the saints,

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness. God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day. God […]
echoes.note: That 'God is not a God of confusion but of peace' (14:33) coheres with the creation account, where God orders the formless and void into structured cosmos. The theology that God's nature opposes chaos draws on the Genesis ordering of creation, though Paul makes no verbal citation; a thematic, contested echo.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh who created the heavens, the God who formed the earth and made it, who established it and didn’t create it a waste, who formed it to be inhabited: “I am Yahweh; and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, in a place of the land of darkness. I didn’t say to the seed of Jacob, ‘Seek me in vain.’ I, Yahweh, speak righteousness. I declare things that are right.
echoes.note: God 'did not create the earth a chaos (tohu)' but formed it to be inhabited and 'did not speak in secret'—a striking pairing of order against chaos with the call to intelligible divine speech that matches both Paul's anti-confusion principle and his demand for understandable worship (14:33, cf. 14:9). The conjunction of these two motifs in the same Isaiah 45 chapter Paul is already mining strengthens the coherence.

pericopes.text: let your wives keep silent in the assemblies, for it has not been permitted for them to speak; but let them be in subjection, as the law also says. If they desire to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to chatter in the assembly. What? Was it from you that the word of God went out? Or did it come to you alone?

echoes.text: To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. In pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”
echoes.note: The command that wives 'be in subjection, as the law also says' (14:34) is widely understood to invoke Genesis 3:16, 'your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you,' the only Torah text grounding wifely subordination. Since Paul cites no chapter, this is the most plausible referent of 'the law,' and it coheres with his appeal to Genesis order elsewhere; volume rests on the allusion to the rule-over-her clause.

echoes.text: Yahweh God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep. As the man slept, he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place. Yahweh God made a woman from the rib which had taken from the man, and brought her to the man. The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.” Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be […]
echoes.note: 'The law' grounding women's submission (14:34) may alternatively reach back to the creation-order of woman from man, which Paul invokes for headship elsewhere. The echo is faint and the referent disputed, but the Genesis 2 sequence is a candidate for the Torah basis Paul assumes.

echoes.text: “Also when a woman vows a vow to Yahweh, and binds herself by a bond, being in her father’s house, in her youth, and her father hears her vow, and her bond with which she has bound her soul, and her father holds his peace at her; then all her vows shall stand, and every bond with which she has bound her soul shall stand. But if her father forbids her in the day that he hears, none of her vows, or of her bonds with which she has bound her soul, shall […]
echoes.note: The Torah's regulation of a wife's vows under her husband's authority offers a possible legal basis for 'as the law also says' regarding wifely subjection (14:34). It is a faint, contested candidate; most read 'the law' as Genesis 3:16, but the vow-law shows the OT availability of wifely submission to the husband's authority.

pericopes.text: If any man thinks himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him recognize the things which I write to you, that they are the commandment of the Lord. But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant. Therefore, brothers, desire earnestly to prophesy, and don’t forbid speaking with other languages. Let all things be done decently and in order.

echoes.text: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: Paul's rebuke, 'Was it from you that the word of God went out?' (14:36) faintly plays on the prophetic conviction that 'out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem'—the word originates from God's chosen center, not from the Corinthians. The link is allusive and contested, but it underlies Paul's claim that the divine word is not theirs to originate.

pericopes.text: Now I declare to you, brothers, the Good News which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand, by which also you are saved, if you hold firmly the word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also. For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was bestowed on me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Whether then it is I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: Paul's creedal 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures' (v.3) draws on the Servant who is 'wounded for our transgressions' and on whom the LORD lays 'the iniquity of us all.' Volume is moderate (no verbatim quotation) but coherence is high: the vicarious sin-bearing death is the only OT text supplying the formula, and Isaiah 53 was a primary resurrection-era proof-text. Availability is secure.

echoes.text: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people? They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth. Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his […]
echoes.note: The Servant 'cut off out of the land of the living,' 'numbered with the transgressors,' who 'bore the sin of many,' and is afterward vindicated ('he shall see... he shall prolong his days') undergirds the death-burial-vindication shape of the kerygma in vv.3-5. Recurrence: Paul appeals to Isaiah 53 elsewhere (Rom 4:25; 10:16). The 'according to the Scriptures' refrain points here for the death.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up' is the strongest single OT candidate for 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures' (v.4), since no other text gives a third-day resurrection. Targumic/rabbinic tradition read Hosea 6:2 of resurrection, supporting availability. Contested because Paul never cites it explicitly and the LXX wording differs.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor let your holy one see corruption' was the apostolic resurrection proof-text (Acts 2:27; 13:35) and plausibly stands behind 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.' Coherence with the burial-then-raising sequence (vv.4) is good; volume is low here since Paul does not quote it. Marked echo, not quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: 'Three days and three nights in the belly of the fish' is a possible scriptural warrant for the third-day timing, read figurally of death and deliverance (cf. Matt 12:40). Volume and recurrence in Paul are nil, so this is a faint, contested figural reading offered only because the 'according to the Scriptures' for the third day demands OT grounding.

pericopes.text: Now if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised. If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith also is in vain. Yes, we are found false witnesses of God, because we testified about God that he raised up Christ, whom he didn’t raise up, if it is so that the dead are not raised. For if the dead aren’t raised, neither has Christ been raised. If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins. Then they also who are fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The argument turns on whether 'the dead are raised'; the language of those 'fallen asleep' (v.18) who would 'perish' if there is no resurrection echoes Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.' Volume is faint and the verse is more clearly invoked later (v.52), so this is a low echo flagging the second-temple resurrection hope animating the whole section.

pericopes.text: But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep. For since death came by man, the resurrection of the dead also came by man. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then those who are Christ’s, at his coming. Then the end comes, when he will deliver up the Kingdom to God, even the Father; when he will have abolished all rule and all authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy that will be abolished is death. For, “He put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when he says, “All things are put in subjection”, it is evident that he is excepted who subjected all things to him. When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son will also himself be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.

echoes.text: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
echoes.note: 'Since death came by man... as in Adam all die' (vv.21-22) presupposes the Eden narrative where the LORD warns 'in the day you eat of it you shall surely die,' the origin of death through the first man. Coherence is very high: the Adam-Christ antithesis is the structural spine of the chapter and recurs at Rom 5:12-21.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: 'You are dust, and to dust you shall return' supplies the mortality that 'in Adam all die' (v.22) names and that the resurrection reverses. The dust motif resurfaces explicitly at vv.47-49, giving recurrence within the chapter and securing coherence.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet' is quoted verbatim in v.27 (LXX Ps 8:7) and expounded as proof that death too must be subjected. Volume is maximal (explicit citation with formula 'for'), and Paul's exegetical attention to 'all things' confirms intentional use. The psalm's 'son of man' enthroned over creation is read christologically.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet' (v.25) fuses Ps 8:6 with 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' The 'enemies under feet' and 'reign until' wording is distinctively Ps 110, the NT's most-cited verse; coherence and recurrence are strong, making this a deliberate conflated allusion.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When you have come into the land which I give to you, and shall reap its harvest, then you shall bring the sheaf of the first fruits of your harvest to the priest: and he shall wave the sheaf before Yahweh, to be accepted for you. On the next day after the Sabbath the priest shall wave it.
echoes.note: 'Christ the first fruits' (vv.20,23) draws on the sheaf of firstfruits waved before the LORD as the pledge of the full harvest. The cultic firstfruits image (cf. Exod 23:19; Deut 26:1-11) coheres with Paul's logic that Christ's rising guarantees the believers' harvest; volume is conceptual rather than verbal, hence echo.

pericopes.text: Or else what will they do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead aren’t raised at all, why then are they baptized for the dead? Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour? I affirm, by the boasting in you which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily. If I fought with animals at Ephesus for human purposes, what does it profit me? If the dead are not raised, then “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Don’t be deceived! “Evil companionships corrupt good morals.” Wake up righteously, and don’t sin, for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

echoes.text: and behold, joy and gladness, killing cattle and killing sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.”
echoes.note: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' is quoted verbatim in v.32 from Isaiah's oracle against Jerusalem's fatalistic revelers. Volume is maximal; Paul deploys it as the logical conclusion of a world without resurrection, matching Isaiah's context of those who ignore the coming judgment. Secure quotation.

echoes.text: Hear Yahweh’s word, you children of Israel; for Yahweh has a charge against the inhabitants of the land: “Indeed there is no truth, nor goodness, nor knowledge of God in the land.
echoes.note: 'Some have no knowledge of God' (v.34) echoes Hosea's indictment 'there is no... knowledge of God in the land' (cf. Hos 4:6, 'my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge'). The prophetic charge of ignorance of God as moral failure coheres with Paul's shaming rebuke; verbal overlap on 'knowledge of God' supports a medium-confidence allusion.

echoes.text: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. The king spoke and said to Daniel, Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you. A stone was brought, and laid on the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel. Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting; neither were instruments of music […]
echoes.note: 'I fought with beasts at Ephesus' (v.32) may be read figurally against Daniel cast among the lions and delivered, the paradigm of the righteous sufferer rescued from beasts. Volume is low and Paul's phrase is likely metaphorical for human adversaries, so this is a faint figural echo of the deliverance-from-beasts tradition.

echoes.text: Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, from the horns of the wild oxen, you have answered me.
echoes.note: 'Save me from the mouth of the lion' belongs to the righteous-sufferer's plea to be rescued from beasts, a possible backdrop to 'I fought with beasts at Ephesus' (v.32). The echo is faint and contested, offered alongside Daniel 6 as the Septuagintal language of beastly threat surrounding the persecuted faithful.

echoes.text: One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm.
echoes.note: The maxim 'Evil companionships corrupt good morals' (v.33) is a Greek proverb (Menander, Thais), but its sense mirrors 'the companion of fools will suffer harm.' Availability as Scripture is the issue: the wording is Hellenistic, so this is a low, contested echo of the wisdom theme rather than a citation of Proverbs.

pericopes.text: But someone will say, “How are the dead raised?” and, “With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish one, that which you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies. That which you sow, you don’t sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, maybe of wheat, or of some other kind. But God gives it a body even as it pleased him, and to each seed a body of its own. All flesh is not the same flesh, but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of animals, another of fish, and another of birds. There are also celestial bodies, and terrestrial bodies; but the glory of the celestial differs from that of the terrestrial. There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for one star differs from another star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body and there is also a spiritual body. So also it is written, “The first man, Adam, became a living soul.” The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. However that which is spiritual isn’t first, but that which is natural, then that which is spiritual. The first man is of the earth, made of dust. The second man is the Lord from heaven. As is the one made of dust, such are those who are also made of dust; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let’s also bear the image of the heavenly.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The first man, Adam, became a living soul' (v.45) quotes Gen 2:7 LXX ('the man became a living soul') verbatim, adding 'first' and 'Adam' to set up the antithesis with the 'last Adam' as life-giving spirit. Volume is maximal with citation formula 'it is written'; this is the chapter's anchoring OT text for the two-Adam anthropology.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The first man is of the earth, made of dust' (v.47) re-reads Gen 2:7, where God forms the man 'of the dust of the ground.' The dust/earth motif distinguishes the earthly Adam from 'the Lord from heaven'; recurrence within vv.45-49 confirms deliberate exegetical use beyond the v.45 citation.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: 'Those who are made of dust' bearing 'the image of the man of dust' (vv.48-49) recalls 'dust you are, and to dust you shall return,' the mortality stamped on Adam's line. It reinforces the Gen 2:7 dust language with the death-sentence of Eden, giving the contrast its weight of perishability.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: 'As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly' (v.49) invokes the creation of humanity 'in the image of God,' now patterned after the heavenly Man. The image (eikon) language is distinctively Gen 1:26-27 (cf. 5:3); coherence with Paul's Adam Christology supports a medium allusion.

echoes.text: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: The graded 'glory' of sun, moon, and differing stars applied to the resurrection body (vv.40-42) echoes 'those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars.' Daniel's astral imagery of the risen righteous gives the star-glory analogy its resurrection coherence; verbal overlap on stars/glory grounds the allusion.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
echoes.note: 'To each seed a body of its own' and the distinct kinds of flesh (vv.38-39) faintly echo the creation account where plants bear seed 'each according to its kind' and creatures are made by kinds. The echo is conceptual, supporting Paul's argument that God assigns distinct bodies; volume is low, hence a faint echo.

pericopes.text: Now I say this, brothers, that flesh and blood can’t inherit the Kingdom of God; neither does the perishable inherit imperishable. Behold, I tell you a mystery. We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed. For this perishable body must become imperishable, and this mortal must put on immortality. But when this perishable body will have become imperishable, and this mortal will have put on immortality, then what is written will happen: “Death is swallowed up in victory.” “Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

echoes.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.
echoes.note: 'Death is swallowed up in victory' (v.54) quotes Isaiah's eschatological banquet oracle, 'he will swallow up death forever.' Paul follows a reading (cf. Theodotion/Aquila) giving 'in victory'; the citation formula 'then shall come to pass the word that is written' marks maximal volume. The text is the OT charter for death's defeat.

echoes.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.
echoes.note: 'Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?' (v.55) quotes Hosea's taunt, 'O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your destruction?' (LXX). Volume is high (verbatim apostrophe to Death), and Paul fuses it with Isaiah 25:8 to climax the resurrection argument. Secure quotation.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'The dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed' (v.52) draws on 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life.' The sleep-then-awake resurrection schema and the transformation of the raised cohere with Daniel's two-outcome resurrection; recurrence of the 'sleep' motif (vv.6,18,51) supports the allusion.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'At the last trumpet... the trumpet will sound' (v.52) echoes the eschatological 'great trumpet' that gathers the scattered to worship. The trumpet as signal of the end-time ingathering of God's people coheres with the resurrection summons; among trumpet texts this is the most eschatologically specific, hence medium.

echoes.text: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand:
echoes.note: 'Blow the trumpet in Zion... for the day of the LORD is coming' is part of the prophetic Day-of-the-LORD trumpet tradition behind 'the last trumpet' (v.52). Volume is low and the motif is diffuse across several prophets, so this is a faint echo alongside Isaiah 27:13 and Zechariah 9:14.

echoes.text: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.
echoes.note: 'The Lord GOD will sound the trumpet' in the theophanic deliverance oracle contributes to the eschatological-trumpet background of v.52. The echo is faint and one of several trumpet texts; included to map the cluster of OT trumpet imagery Paul compresses into 'the last trumpet.'

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled.
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany 'trumpet blast' that summons Israel before God may stand at the headwaters of the eschatological trumpet of v.52. Volume is low and the link is typological rather than verbal, so this is a faint echo of the trumpet-of-divine-presence tradition.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality;
echoes.note: 'This mortal must put on immortality' (vv.53-54) resonates with the deuterocanonical hope that 'the souls of the righteous... their hope is full of immortality.' Availability as second-temple text is secure; the verbal link on immortality (athanasia) is real but the conceptual frame differs (Paul stresses bodily transformation), so a low, contested echo.

pericopes.text: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I commanded the assemblies of Galatia, you do likewise. On the first day of the week, let each one of you save, as he may prosper, that no collections be made when I come. When I arrive, I will send whoever you approve with letters to carry your gracious gift to Jerusalem. If it is appropriate for me to go also, they will go with me.

echoes.text: Every man shall give as he is able, according to Yahweh your God’s blessing which he has given you.
echoes.note: Paul directs each one to save 'as he may prosper'—an almost verbatim conceptual match to Deuteronomy's pilgrim-feast rule that each give 'as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God which he has given you.' The volume is high at the level of the proportional-giving principle, and the festal-collection setting (cf. Pentecost in v.8) increases coherence.

echoes.text: And the feast of harvest, the first fruits of your labors, which you sow in the field; and the feast of ingathering, at the end of the year, when you gather in your labors out of the field.
echoes.note: The weekly setting-aside of gifts on the first day evokes the agricultural firstfruits/ingathering offerings of the festal calendar. The link is thematic (sanctified periodic giving) rather than verbal, so volume is low and it is partly carried by Paul's later 'firstfruits' language in v.15.

echoes.text: Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase:
echoes.note: 'Honor the LORD with your substance and with the firstfruits of all your produce' undergirds Paul's appeal to set aside wealth for sacred use. Verbal contact is faint and the proverb is one of several wisdom sources for proportional generosity, so confidence stays low.

pericopes.text: But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia, for I am passing through Macedonia. But with you it may be that I will stay, or even winter, that you may send me on my journey wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now in passing, but I hope to stay a while with you, if the Lord permits. But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

echoes.text: I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: Paul's 'a great and effective door has opened to me' may draw on the prophetic 'door of hope' that the LORD opens for renewed mission. The metaphor of a divinely-opened door for fruitful action has OT antecedents, but the contact is conceptual not verbal and the open-door image is broadly diffuse, so it is contested.

pericopes.text: Now if Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear, for he does the work of the Lord, as I also do. Therefore let no one despise him. But set him forward on his journey in peace, that he may come to me; for I expect him with the brothers. Now concerning Apollos, the brother, I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; and it was not at all his desire to come now; but he will come when he has an opportunity.
Watch! Stand firm in the faith! Be courageous! Be strong! Let all that you do be done in love.

echoes.text: Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who hope in Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD' is the closest verbal and structural parallel to Paul's paired imperatives 'be courageous, be strong.' Volume is high (LXX andrizesthe/krataiousthe vocabulary matches), and the exhortation-to-the-faithful setting gives strong coherence.

echoes.text: “Be strong and courageous; for you shall cause this people to inherit the land which I swore to their fathers to give them. Only be strong and very courageous, to observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may […]
echoes.note: The repeated divine charge 'be strong and courageous' to Joshua is the canonical fountainhead of the formula Paul echoes. The LXX renders it with the same andrizou/ischye verbs Paul uses, giving high volume and strong recurrence across the courage-tradition.

echoes.text: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.” Moses called to Joshua, and said to him in the sight of all Israel, “Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land which Yahweh has sworn to their fathers to give them; and you shall cause them to inherit it.
echoes.note: Moses' twofold 'be strong and courageous' to Israel and to Joshua belongs to the same exhortation cluster, sharing LXX vocabulary with Paul's imperatives. It is one of several courage-formula texts, so it ranks just below the Joshua/Psalm 31 parallels in distinctiveness.

echoes.text: Be courageous, and let us be strong for our people, and for the cities of our God; and Yahweh do that which seems good to him.”
echoes.note: Joab's battle exhortation 'Be strong, and let us be courageous for our people' supplies the martial coloring of 'act like men' (andrizesthe). The military-valor sense reinforces coherence with Paul's call to firm faith, though it is one node in a recurring formula.

echoes.text: Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage' is a near-twin of Psalm 31:24 and feeds the same exhortation tradition Paul reuses. High recurrence within the Psalter strengthens the case, though it overlaps heavily with the Psalm 31 parallel.

pericopes.text: Now I beg you, brothers (you know the house of Stephanas, that it is the first fruits of Achaia, and that they have set themselves to serve the saints), that you also be in subjection to such, and to everyone who helps in the work and labors. I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus; for that which was lacking on your part, they supplied. For they refreshed my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge those who are like that.

echoes.text: that you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you shall bring in from your land that Yahweh your God gives you. You shall put it in a basket, and shall go to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there.
echoes.note: Calling the household of Stephanas 'the firstfruits of Achaia' applies the Deuteronomic firstfruits rite—the first of the produce consecrated to God—figurally to the first converts of a region. Volume rests on the loaded term 'firstfruits' (aparche), and the consecration-of-the-first logic gives genuine coherence.

echoes.text: Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase:
echoes.note: The firstfruits-to-God motif of Proverbs reinforces Paul's honorific use of 'firstfruits' for the Stephanas household and their dedicated service. The link is thematic and secondary to the Deuteronomic rite, so confidence is low.

pericopes.text: The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Priscilla greet you much in the Lord, together with the assembly that is in their house. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. This greeting is by me, Paul, with my own hand.
If any man doesn’t love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed. Come, Lord! The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love to all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

echoes.text: ‘Cursed is the man who makes an engraved or molten image, an abomination to Yahweh, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and sets it up in secret.’ All the people shall answer and say, ‘Amen.’ ‘Cursed is he who dishonors his father or his mother.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’ ‘Cursed is he who removes his neighbor’s landmark.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’ ‘Cursed is he who leads the blind astray on the road.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’ […]
echoes.note: Paul's 'let him be accursed' (anathema) on whoever does not love the Lord reflects the Deuteronomic covenant-curse liturgy, where the assembly pronounces 'cursed' on covenant-breakers. The setting—a closing covenantal sanction against the disloyal—gives coherence, though the conceptual rather than verbal contact keeps it medium.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'Maranatha / Come, Lord!' invokes the eschatological coming of the Lord, of which Malachi's 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' is a prime OT expectation. The contact is thematic (the awaited advent that judges the disloyal), pairing naturally with the preceding curse, so it is offered low and contested.

echoes.text: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.
echoes.note: 'He comes to judge the earth' frames the Lord's advent that Paul's Maranatha petitions, joining curse and coming in a judgment horizon. Diffuse OT advent-language and absence of verbal markers keep this faint and contested.
